    #147957. Tech Report: Expert Tips for Patterning and Hunting a Late-Season Buck

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1203 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Expert Tips for Patterning and Hunting a Late-Season Buck

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1203 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Beaten, bruised, and a bit smarter than it was on opening day, the old buck slowly moves from his bed.
    • Keeping it in low gear, the deer alternates between taking a couple steps and scanning its surroundings.
    • Sitting high in a tall cedar tree, you wait for any sign of the major 10-pointer you’ve been after all season.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Beaten, bruised, and a bit smarter than it was on opening day, the old buck slowly moves from his bed. The sun just set, but he’s not anywhere close to a big field yet.

    Keeping it in low gear, the deer alternates between taking a couple steps and scanning its surroundings. On pins and pine needles, the buck nears the edge of the bedding area, hits a smaller trail other deer rarely use, and sets course for the distant standing soybean field.

    Sitting high in a tall cedar tree, you wait for any sign of the major 10-pointer you’ve been after all season. Any moment now….

    In a recent development, suddenly, you see the front legs of a deer standing in the timber on the hill above. Seconds turn into minutes, and the deer doesn’t move. Finally, it covers a few more yards, and that significant 10-point rack comes into view. Only 50 yards separate the late-season hunter and the buck — all because he focused on patterning a late-season buck. Here’s how to do it.

    Recent findings suggest that some elements of patterning a late-season deer take place before the hunt. It’s a good time to reassess the situation, reflect on the past, and take a new approach.

    It has been revealed that hunt fresh spots. Late-season deer are especially wary. At this point in the season, some deer have been shot and shot at. Virtually all deer have felt pressure, so it’s crucial to spend some time scouting areas that weren’t hunted previously. Oftentimes, it’s these places deer slink into during the late season. Even if these spots seem less than perfect, it’s worth scouting them.

    Reflect on the Past: Consider past seasons and how deer behaved then. Refer to trail camera intel and sightings of deer in the field. Digging into the details of past seasons will help you understand current and future deer movement. If conditions and habitat factors and food sources line up similarly to how they have in the past, deer should exhibit similar patterns. This takes a lot of the guesswork out of game planning.

    Sources indicate that effective deer hunting is all about knowing whitetail lines of movement. Studying the lines that take whitetails from point A to point B is crucial for selecting a high-odds stand or blind location.

    It has been revealed that locate the food. Food drives late-season deer behavior. Locate the food, and you find the deer. That noted, deer place emphasis on the limiting resource factor. If safe bedding cover is scarce, they’ll find what’s available and travel farther to reach food. If safe bedding cover is abundant, they’ll bed closer to the available food.

    Hunt a late-season kill plot. It’s too late to plant now, but if you planted a late-season food plot, it’s time to cash in. Standing corn, standing soybeans, winter wheat, turnips, and much more, make excellent late-season food sources for whitetails. Placing a winter food plot in a strategic location, such as near solar or thermal bedding cover, is a solid play. It can make the patterning process much easier.

    According to recent reports, save a food plot. As fall gives way to winter, and food sources wane, deer hammer what’s left. The only way to keep a food plot viable into the late season is to prevent deer and other critters from consuming it earlier. That requires planting the right plant species (like brassicas), keeping deer out (with an electric exclusion fence), and opening it up at just the right time. Thus, you’re saving a food plot for the final days of the season.

    Find the thermal bedding. Deer use certain types of bedding cover to combat the winter cold. The most common is thermal bedding (especially in flatter areas without much topography). This comes in the form of cedars, spruce, and pine trees. These evergreens shield deer from the rain, sleet, and snow. Furthermore, these thick plants block bitter-cold winds. Equally impressive is that the air temperature is several degrees warmer amidst the conifers.

    Identify south-facing slopes. Deer also benefit significantly from the sun. Because the winter sun rises in the southeast, and sets in the southwest, the southerly face of the slope will be warmer on sunny days. So long as deer aren’t pressured there, it should be the primary deer bedding spot for the general area.

    Sources indicate that glass from afar. Even in today’s world of cellular trail cameras, the age-old tactic of sitting down and raising the glasses is still a good one. You’ll need open country like fields that serve as primary food sources.

    Recent findings suggest that watch a buck’s route. To pattern a deer is to know its general whereabouts and habits. These include bedding areas, food sources, water sources, staging areas, and the travel routes in between. By watching a buck’s route in person, scouting for tracks, or monitoring via trail cameras, hunters can watch a buck’s route and make firm intends after identifying the target.

    According to recent reports, reposition trail cameras. While in the field scouting for deer sign, positioning stands, filling feeders, and completing other tasks, go ahead and set up some new trail camera locations. Where legal, focus on the cellular variety. If cameras that were productive early season have gone dead now, don’t be afraid to move them to more promising spots.

    After determining your target buck’s lines of movement, it’s time to make a move. Put the initiative in motion, or call an audible as needed.

    It has been revealed that still hunt the edges. While still hunting works best during the rut when deer are more distracted, it can be effective during the late season, too. If you’ve had trouble patterning a late-season buck, consider still hunting. Moving slowly, yet covering ground, might help piece together remaining clues to hunt a deer you know about, or help find a upcoming one altogether. Still hunting is especially effective for morning hunts, when it’s often difficult to hike straight into a stand location without spooking deer.

    Read Next: The Case for Ditching Your Treestand and Hunting from the Ground.

    In a recent development, track down your buck. A fresh blanket of snow makes for prime tracking conditions, and if you have an idea about a buck’s travel lines, tracking becomes a lot easier. Go slow, and keep your eyes peeled. Chances are good he’ll see you first, but move slowly enough, and you’ll have a chance at a shot.

    In a recent development, be mobile and flexible. Whether you are hunting from a treestand, hunting blind, or still hunting through cover, remember to be flexible. Be patient and execute your plan, but don’t be so attached that it stays in motion even after it becomes clear another tactic is better. Remember that each deer hunt is its own unique experience. Thus, hunters should always implement tactics based on the situation.

    Late-season deer hunting is no cakewalk. Deer are skittish and the bitter cold can be tough to endure. Nonetheless, hunt hard, and you just might bag a buck. Focus on new, unpressured spots, protected bedding areas, and primary food sources to finally punch that buck tag.

    Tech Report: We Forgot the Thanksgiving Turkey. So We Went Striper Fishing Instead

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This story, “Striped Turkey,” appeared in the November 1955 concern of Outdoor Life.
    • Five minutes after the arrival of my Boston brother and his family at my home in East Hampton, Connecticut, we discovered a calamity.
    • We thought they were to bring it, and they thought we were to get it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This story, “Striped Turkey,” appeared in the November 1955 concern of Outdoor Life.

    Five minutes after the arrival of my Boston brother and his family at my home in East Hampton, Connecticut, we discovered a calamity. Neither of us had bought a turkey, and it was already 10 o’clock Thanksgiving Eve.

    We thought they were to bring it, and they thought we were to get it.

    Above the hysterical babble, I made a daring suggestion: “Maybe we can make do with something else.”.

    “Nonsense,” my wife snorted. “What would you like? Cranberry sauce, mashed potatoes, pumpkin pie, and beans?”.

    Brother Don raised a hand commanding silence.

    According to recent reports, “This is probably the best thing that could have happened,” he remarked. “Be a good lesson for the kids. Teach them to be resourceful. Now I have a plan. . . .”.

    According to recent reports, “That’s crazy,” I interrupted as I saw his eyes fixed on my old single-shot .22 standing in the corner. “There hasn’t been a turkey shot in Connecticut for 200 years.”.

    Industry observers note that “I wasn’t planning to hunt. You and I were figuring on fishing in the morning, right?” he asked.

    “O.K.,” he remarked, “it’s simple, instead of fishing just for sport, we fish to eat.”.

    “That’s out!” both wives screamed.

    Sources indicate that “For weeks the children have been learning about Thanksgiving in school,” Cynthia informed us. “They’ve drawn pictures of turkeys, talked about turkeys, and written poems about turkeys. And it just won’t be Thanksgiving without a turkey.”.

    “That’s silly,” I replied. “If you figure that way, then we’ve got to find some Indians, too.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “Sure,” Don added. “That bird guff is just propaganda cooked up by the turkey growers.”.

    “I’ll bet, if the truth were known, the pilgrims ate striped bass instead of turkey,” I said.

    “Of course they did,” Don noted. He rubbed his hands in satisfaction. “It’s all settled now. You girls sleep late in the morning and leave everything to us. We’ll be back by noon with a striper.”.

    “We’ll get some scallops while we’re at it, too,” I promised.

    “Even some oysters,” Don injected.

    Recent findings suggest that the kids were snake dancing from room to room and shouting a song about gobble, gobble, gobblers as they went. The wives stood around, looking incredulous, so Don felt it necessary to add a clincher. When I got the drift of what he was proposing I gave him a kick, but it was too late. He promised that if we weren’t back by 1 o’clock — with the fish — we’d all go out to a fine restaurant for dinner.

    When we were alone I told him, “You didn’t have to promise that. The bill for this mob will sink us.”.

    In a recent development, “Nonsense. Have some confidence. We’ll catch fish,” he countered.

    In a recent development, it was still dark when we left the house next morning, and you could smell the cold — just before your nostrils were pinched shut. While the car engine warmed up, I dashed back into the house, made some instant coffee, and poured it into a vacuum bottle. I must have awakened my sleeping wife.

    Industry observers note that “Take your time,” she called from upstairs. “We’ll be dressed and ready to go at 1 o’clock.”.

    Sources indicate that in addition to our tackle, we stuck a long-handled scallop net into the car. Neither Don nor I said much as we drove the 25 miles to Niantic, where I keep my boat. He kept fiddling with the radio, tuning in each station’s weather report, no doubt figuring that eventually he’d hear a report that promised “fair and rapidly rising temperatures.”.

    According to recent reports, I mulled over our chances for getting fish and the subject of frostbite striper fishing in general. Most of the bass caught in Connecticut are the small, school fish. During the warmer months these 2 to 10-pounders look like mighty small potatoes, compared to the 40 and 50-pounders taken in other coastal states. We get our compensation in the winter, when the giant bass of neighboring states have taken off for warmer climes. Our stripers stay with us. They’re natives and provide fishing in even the coldest weather. It’s surprising how large a 10-pound fish looks in the month of January.

    Sources indicate that when we arrived at the dock it was still dark, but my boat gleamed ghostlike in a heavy shroud of frost. Ice lay thick in the bottom.

    Hot spot for this refrigerated striper angling is in the southeast corner of the state, in the Thames and Niantic rivers. In the past I got action almost 50 percent of the time. That is, every second trip I stood a good chance of taking fish. Unfortunately, that reckoning doomed this Thanksgiving-Day trip from the start, for I’d done very well the last time out. But then, who wants to quit when they’re ahead?

    When we arrived at the dock it was still dark, but my boat gleamed ghostlike in a heavy shroud of frost. Ice lay thick in the bottom. I realized my boating season was about over. I’d have to haul it out within a few days, for the intermittent thaws and freezes hurt a boat. And anyway, most winter bass fishing is done from shore.

    Instead of using a bailing can, Don chipped away on the ice with a screwdriver, while I attached the motor to the stern and loaded our gear. By the time we were under way, the sun had begun to light up the undersides of long, stringy clouds.

    “Where shall we start operations?” I asked.

    “Play the hunches,” Don suggested. “What goes with Thanksgiving?”.

    According to recent reports, “O.K.,” I stated, and swung the boat in the direction of Turkey Point, the most popular spot on the Niantic River. At that early hour we would have the place to ourselves. Speeding along, our boat left the slightly rippled surface of the channel and entered an area that looked somewhat like an oil slick.

    It was ice — a microscopically thin glaze of the stuff.

    “This will cut our lines,” he warned.

    In a recent development, I told him I didn’t think so. “It’s so thin, and it doesn’t seem to be around the point.”.

    In a recent development, A stronger current there had evidently prevented the ice formation. I killed the motor and we started casting to the deep water that lay along the edge of a submerged sandbar.

    Recent findings suggest that there are two popular and proven techniques used in the Niantic for stripers. One is to troll sand or bloodworms behind spinner blades, and the other is casting (usually with spinning tackle) white, weighted bucktails. These are often used with a trailing pork strip. We had worms, lures and tackle to exploit either system.

    In a recent development, it was still bitter cold and the sun hadn’t made much progress harvesting our crop of frost. We cast with extra vigor to get warm.

    Several other boats raced up the river, as though in fear we were cleaning out the fish. One boat eased up to within 50 feet of us, put out a trolling line, and before the worm was decently moist, had hooked a fish.

    “How do you like that!” Don moaned as we watched a five-pounder swung aboard. “We’ve been here for an hour and haven’t even had a strike.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “Maybe it’s going to take trolling to score this morning,” I remarked. I brought my bucktail in and prepared to fix a trolling rig.

    In a recent development, I glanced up and saw that another fellow in a different boat with a bowing rod — right where we’d drifted through. We watched his line slicing the water, and finally the flashing silver as he netted his catch.

    “It isn’t just the trollers that are getting fish,” Don said.

    I decided to stick with casting. I tried every retrieve I could think of — slow, fast, and in between; with action and without.

    It has been revealed that it had warmed up enough to shed one layer of clothing. The warmth was welcome, but each passing minute meant we were that much nearer our 1 o’clock deadline.

    “Maybe we’re fishing too fast,” Don remarked. “Possibly, because so much depends on it, we’re rushing our retrieves.”.

    “That’s ridiculous,” I argued. “We’ve been trying everything.”.

    Sources indicate that we couldn’t keep our eyes off the other boats. By then there were about a dozen, some trolling, others drifting as their occupants cast. Stripers were being caught by everyone, so it seemed, but us.

    In a recent development, “This is justice,” Don groaned. “Here these guys are fishing for fun. They’ll go home, dump their fish into an icebox, mix a Martini, then sit down to a turkey dinner, while we . . .” he shrugged hopelessly.

    It has been revealed that “It doesn’t make sense,” I added. “We’re using the same lures, fishing the same water, and as fishermen we’re at least as good as they are.”.

    Sources indicate that “Don’t place any bets on that,” Don kidded. “Let’s try trolling.”.

    We rigged up one line to go deep and the other to work shallow. I regulated the speed of the boat so the long sandworms trailed enticingly. Then, remembering a trip when a different technique had paid off, I rigged an extra outfit and stuck a shapeless gob of worms on that hook.

    It has been revealed that time was passing; it was after 9:30 when we started trolling. We headed upriver. An acquaintance of mine was trolling downriver, and we killed motors to exchange confidences.

    “Pretty good,” I answered. “How’re you doing?”.

    “Pretty good. Got three or four — sort of slowing up now, though. Guess early in the morning is best.” My friend started his motor and waved farewell.

    Don was fit to be tied. “Imagine that,” he stated. “Three or four fish. Can’t he count? Is he a liar? ‘Sort of slowing up now,’ the man said. Well, anyway, for us things can’t get any slower.” Don disgustedly yanked his rod and started reeling in the line that had sunk to the bottom while we were talking. Suddenly his rod tip started twitching. “Holy cow!” he yelled. “I’ve got a fish.”.

    Recent findings suggest that A second later he shook his head as the line came in too easily. “Guess not. Probably just some weed.”.

    He kept reeling and landed the smallest, most ridiculous-looking flatfish I’ve ever seen. He held it up in brief contempt before tossing it back. Lady luck wasn’t just ignoring us, she was giving us the bird.

    All morning we’d noticed two men in a bright-green runabout who were having frequent action. Now, as they trolled by, I saw the chap at the motor slyly drop something over the stern.

    “They’re chumming. I bet that’s the answer,” Don said. “I’ve seen it done before. Bits of worm are tossed over, the bass pick these up as appetizers, and when the large trolled worm comes by they grab it.”.

    “Should we give it a try?” I asked.

    Sources indicate that “We haven’t enough worms. Besides, others around here catch fish without chumming.”.

    I looked at my watch — 10 o’clock. We’d been fishing almost five hours with nothing to show but Don’s flatfish.

    “Do you suppose any of these people would sell a couple —” A tremendous yank on my line shut me up fast. I reached down and snapped the motor into neutral. It stalled and suddenly everything was as quiet as a house without a TV set. Then I thought I heard the taut monofilament sizzling through the water, but it was my own excited breathing.

    I knew it was a good fish. I loosened the drag to let it run, and the fish took my line in a wide circle around the boat. We were in the middle of the river and I couldn’t see anything around to cause a snag. All I had to do was keep my head. To be safe, I loosened the drag some more. And then, unbridled, the fish really took off.

    “Put some weight on him!” Don yelled.

    Industry observers note that “Just keep cool and take it easy,” I kept telling myself. Using finger pressure against the spool, I brought the fish to a sluggish stop. I started pumping the rod and it felt as if I were bringing the heavy boat to the fish rather than the fish to the boat.

    “It’s a good one.” Don had seen it.

    Sources indicate that then I saw it, and it was a beauty. Don had the net deep in the water, and I held my breath as I led the tugging striper to him. With a “wooosh” of the net, the fish was ours. I let my breath go and flopped down on my open tackle box, immune to the pain of an upturned 8/0 hook.

    It has been revealed that the fish pulled the pointer of my pocket scale below the 12-pound mark — the heaviest striped bass I’ve taken from that river. It was large enough for our requirements, and since time was at a premium, we decided to go after the scallops.

    We gunned the boat back to the dock to get one of the 15¢ permits entitling you to one bushel of Niantic scallops. These scallops are considered a delicacy throughout Connecticut. The season opens in October, and by Thanksgiving the beds have been well worked over.

    The technique for taking these shellfish is basically simple — one merely uses the long-handled net as a scoop over the bottom. Luck and skill determine the percentage of scallops in a net full of mud, seaweed, empty shells, and stones.

    Industry observers note that luck played on our side for a change, and we came across an area where Don made one productive scoop after another. Within 30 minutes we had all we needed.

    In a recent development, “We’re really cooking now,” Don mentioned. “How about the oysters?”.

    I looked at my watch. “Suits me. The tide will be just about right.”.

    The oysters we had in mind were the small, rock variety that are found at low tide along stony beaches. We decided on a place a few miles down the coast, where we usually had good luck before. We moored the boat, got our gear, fish, and scallops into the car, and were on our way.

    “I’m starving,” Don noted. “Can we stop for a hamburger?”.

    Industry observers note that I shook my head. “Nope, we’re running a tight schedule. It’s 11:30 already.”.

    Sources indicate that this beach, like most of the Connecticut shoreline at this season, was deserted, the cottages boarded up. The day, by that time, was warm, and the sun made sand and water glisten with midsummer gaiety. It was a particularly low tide, and when we got to the rocky point we found oysters aplenty.

    I was carrying a sack, but it was several minutes before anything went in it. With drawn knives and the appetites of shipwrecked sailors, we fell upon the oysters. Eaten right on the spot, the clean, saline taste is something you don’t ever get enough of. Oysters disappeared as fast as popcorn at a western movie.

    We finally snapped out of this orgy and gathered stuffing for our bag.

    Sources indicate that we arrived home with five minutes to spare and everyone went to work. The women got busy in the kitchen, while Don and I opened oysters. The older kids readied the scallops. Soon the perfume of baking bass hinted at what was to come. By this time, the kids had forgotten all about turkeys.

    It has been revealed that our first course was oysters on the half shell, followed by generous helpings of scallops, broiled in butter. Then came the bass — baked a delicate brown on the outside, fat with chestnut stuffing inside. It’s true there were no drumsticks to fight over, but on the other hand, there was no neck or tail.

    Afterward, Don lay back on a couch and — after giving a gentle pat to his mid-section — noted, “You know, this dinner was terrific, but next year we can improve on it.”.

    “We’ll take the kids along, and while you and I are out snagging striped turkey, they can dig clams for a chowder.”.

    #147953. Industry News: Old-School Wisdom for Deer Hunting During Snowstorms

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2690 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Old-School Wisdom for Deer Hunting During Snowstorms

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Most whitetail hunters agree that a snowfall is nice for hunting deer.
    • I used to have a recipe for deer tracks, only it wasn’t very filling.
    • Hunters tend to forget that tracks show where whitetails have been — not where they are.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Most whitetail hunters agree that a snowfall is nice for hunting deer. “Look at all the tracks you’ll see with snow covering the ground,” they chorus.

    I used to have a recipe for deer tracks, only it wasn’t very filling.

    Hunters tend to forget that tracks show where whitetails have been — not where they are. And tracks may not necessarily indicate where deer are likely to be again. One deer can make a lot of tracks.

    But if you know how snowfall changes a whitetail’s daily routine, you are starting to understand where you will find tracks — and the deer that made them.

    Let’s rehearse some basic facts.

    First, snow normally comes late in most states’ deer seasons. That means whitetails already have been harassed by other hunters. Unless you hunt private land, all deer you are likely to encounter may be wary, even downright spooky. They are moving little during daylight hours. Rutting bucks are probably limiting much of their roaming to the darkness of night.

    It has been revealed that second, snowstorms — and most other storms — are accompanied by periods of intensely low barometric pressure. Whitetails tend to roam wide in search of food prior to a storm. But they hole up when snow actually starts to fall. And they stay holed up until the storm passes or at least until it eases off.

    Third, while snow means hunters can see deer moving much more easily, it also works the other way around. Deer see the hunter coming a lot farther off. The fact that snow silences the woods forces deer to use their eyes more. Ever spend an hour or two watching a band of deer bedded down after a snowstorm? Their heads are lifted much more often to eyeball the surrounding terrain. Eyes must assume a vigil which ears can no longer accomplish and must provide the essential early warning. Incidentally, your own hearing abilities aren’t helped by snowfall, either. Deer that rustled the crisp frozen leaves of a frosty fall morning won’t be heard walking through a soft cover of upcoming-fallen snow.

    According to recent reports, fourth, snow changes whitetail eating habits — particularly heavy snowfall. Meadow grasses may not be pawed at again until spring. Buds, twigs and surviving leafy vegetation take its place. These plants are less nutritious for deer but they are easier to obtain. Waste grains in fields blown clear of snow may promote a concentration of feeding whitetails.

    So now you are thinking that snowfall might not be such a boon to hunting?

    Actually, it is — if you know how to use it to your advantage.

    Recent findings suggest that whitetails, like all wildlife, are creatures of habit. You can predict a deer’s general reaction to things that impact on its environment. Maybe your predictions won’t be precise but they can be close enough to cut down on the number of fruitless hunting efforts you make.

    Recent findings suggest that pay attention to the weatherman. Be sure you are out hunting on the day before a storm is forecast to arrive. Through changes in barometric pressure, deer sense the oncoming storm. They often move out to feed as heavily as possible — even in the middle of the day — forgoing the usual bedding hours in their hasty urge to stock up before the storm. So be sure to hunt all day.

    Industry observers note that pre-storm is the time to concentrate on checking food sources for whitetails. Hunting pressure earlier in the season may have forced the animals to visit open grainfields only at night. If hunter numbers have dwindled — as they do in most states after the first four or five days of the season — start checking those fields again at dawn and dusk. The urge to fill up before a storm may have deer less cautious.

    In woodland areas, check hidden openings or meadow edges where wild herbaceous cover remains. Don’t overlook timber cuttings where saplings provide cover and the lack of an overstory promotes the undergrowth that deer savor. Try the creek bottoms where frost may not have killed the green grasses yet.

    In farmlands, glass the local hay fields or even vegetable patches where potatoes, sugar beets, carrots, turnips or other root-type plants have not all been harvested yet. And visit abandoned orchards where fallen fruit may provide an attraction.

    It has been revealed that more than once in a late deer season afternoon, while driving the back roads of farm country near where I live, I have become aware of more and more deer suddenly appearing where few were before. The back edge of a cutover hay field will hold five or six deer, all feeding near a heavy hickory and oak woodlot. Harvested cornfields may have a few animals wandering along, plucking up the waste dumped by corn pickers before it can be plowed under.

    In a recent development, does tend to move farther from cover than bucks, particularly when feeding in daylight hours prior to a storm. But expect surprises. Once, while walking across a partially harvested cornfield to reach a gun blind in the woodlot beyond, I stumbled across a fine eight-point buck. This lone deer, feeding in a 12-row patch of standing corn, was fully 80 yards from the nearest heavy cover. He evidently felt safe among the withered cornstalks. And their rattling in the wind had probably masked the sound of my approach.

    I was so startled, in fact, that I never got off a shot from the slug-loaded 12-gauge that I was carrying. The buck wheeled and bounded away before I could shoot.

    In a recent development, don’t be caught unprepared. You never know where a deer will suddenly appear. I’ve had does dart from brushy drainage ditches — deep ones that were mostly dry or had the damp patches frozen solid by late fall’s icy weather. Ditches provide perfect cover routes to reach open stretches with food. Shelterbelts do so, too.

    Sources indicate that once a storm of some magnitude starts, deer simply disappear. Whitetails of both sexes will head for the thickest most protective cover around. Conifers are ideal (pine plantations or cedar swamps in the North Country). In farmlands, overgrown brushy woodlots or thick river bottom or creekbottom cover is an alternative. Here deer will lie down and, unless disturbed by a hunter wandering around in the storm, they will not get up for hours — maybe days.

    The hollow hair in deer’s coats provides superb insulation from the snow’s cold and dampness. Curled up into a small oval (judge for yourself how compactly a whitetail can curl up by the sizes of the beds you’ll find a day or so later) deer will ride out the storm, sometimes allowing the snowfall to almost literally cover them. They don’t seek food and they don’t move much — even to stand and stretch.

    Because hunters don’t normally slog around in heavy storms, deer are usually undisturbed until the snowfall begins to lessen. If a storm lasts more than a day, deer may move around close to their bedding areas but they won’t venture far.

    It is an ideal time, once the storm begins to subside, to mount a deer drive.

    Pinpointing whitetail cover won’t be difficult, even with the lack of tracks on new-fallen snow. Just pick the heaviest thickest junk around. Match the size of the cover to the number of drivers and standers you have with you, and you should be able to fill several tags for your group.

    Recent findings suggest that there is a farmland county near my Michigan home which is a mixture of cedar swamp, brushy woodlots and grainfields, plus some pastureland. Every other season or so, myself and about five of my hunting buddies drive over there on a Saturday. At this time, we’ve all just come back from the North Country’s season opener; perhaps half of us have been fortunate enough to have scored on a buck already. The lucky ones drive for their less successful counterparts.

    In a recent development, through the years, we have secured hunting permission by telephone and by long acquaintance with the local landowners, some of whom join us for these drives. Because this area is open to the use of high-power rifles, it takes only about three or four standers to cover all downwind and sidewind exit routes in the cover we visit.

    Industry observers note that the remainder of us cast back and forth in a line — more or less — of drivers, working silently in the belief that noise startles deer even more than human scent and sends them into headlong flight. We want the whitetails to break cover in a nervous trot, glancing back over their shoulders, not fleeing at top speed.

    Because the drivers move and the deer focus their attention on them, the standers get some easy shots. Standers are urged to find natural blinds that will camouflage just a bit of the brilliance of the Blaze Orange garments they wear.

    It has been revealed that drivers wear as much Blaze Orange as possible for high visibility. They don’t carry firearms, either, on our drives.

    Such minidrives have proved extremely successful. In those years when we all fill tags up north and don’t proposal to visit this county, local landowners call us to see if we’re coming over to help them. It has become a social event. We do go, of course.

    It has been revealed that well-conducted drives, frankly, are one of the best ways to kill whitetails all season long — early or late, in snow or without it. If you develop a compatible group of hunters who are all safety conscious, driving may well be the best way to hunt.

    Industry observers note that for the single hunter, stillhunting in the snow can prove difficult. The muffling effect snow has on sounds is appealing to stillhunters but they should remember that whitetails bedded in snow can be extremely watchful. That’s true at least while a storm is waning or before the sun reappears with warmth enough to prompt more movement of deer. Whitetails scan their surroundings intently. And because they are not likely to be moving, spotting them will prove that much tougher.

    Industry observers note that if a stillhunter is extremely patient and slow moving, maybe he has a chance. But the average hunter who enjoys some success stillhunting on bare ground may find snowy days beyond his capability.

    In a recent development, there is another factor making things tougher: wind. Snowstorms are often accompanied by high winds, ones that don’t die off when the snow stops falling. Wind makes all wildlife nervous. Their hearing isn’t as useful. Add that problem to the noise-muffling effect snow already has and you come up with doubly watchful whitetails.

    So what about doing what you sometimes hear old-timers describe? Just plant yourself on a big buck’s track and walk him into the ground.

    It has been revealed that unless you are a true woodsman, which most of us have neither the time nor the inclination to be, forget it. It sounds rather romantic, as the old sporting books told it, but the method isn’t likely to be very rewarding for the hunter of average skill. Oh, it can be done. And every so often you could be lucky enough to actually walk up on a buck — if you can first figure out which tracks belong to bucks and which belong to does. No, the average lone hunter faced with a snowstorm is better off doing just what the deer do: Wait it out.

    Once the storm passes, whitetails will begin to circulate once again. Hunger drives them from their beds but sunny weather after a storm seems to invigorate deer, too. No scientific facts back up this phenomenon and I claim no insight into the psychology of deer. It’s just a gut feeling I have about whitetails based on observations of the ways yearlings almost cavort after a storm passes. Young bucks, not part of the serious breeding process that is probably about over when snow begins to fall, seem to want to spar. They push each other around rather good naturedly. The older does concentrate on finding food. Now’s the time for the smart single hunter to be on his stand or in his blind.

    Sources indicate that surprisingly, there’s little need to hurry in the morning, either. Deer must feel the cold to some degree because they seldom stir at the crack of dawn after a very cold night. That fact doesn’t mean a hunter shouldn’t be out before daybreak — as he would be earlier in the season. Some whitetails may be stirring. But many times after a storm I’ve witnessed deer waiting until the sun was shining full upon them, waiting for an hour or more after daylight, before moving out to feed. It’s as if they were lying there, soaking up the warmth of the sun.

    As a result, deer will often be feeding — or moving to and from feeding areas — in the middle of the day after the return of good weather conditions. For the man in a blind, deer moving on snow in full daylight are easy to spot.

    Remember, also, that bedding areas on southern exposures — places where the effects of the warm sun are felt the most intensely — will be favored by deer. Anytime the temperature is under 35°, deer seem to prefer places where the sun can hit them in the morning. If it is out of prevailing winds, so much the better.

    Industry observers note that unlike the majority of Western mule deer, which must move from higher mountain summer range to the valleys each winter, whitetails normally find everything they need to survive in a year-round home. One exception is Michigan’s Upper Peninsula where deer summering in the Lake Superior watershed tend to wander southward toward the more temperate climate of Lake Michigan in late fall and early winter, often before deer season ends. Snowfall prompts even greater movement.

    According to recent reports, A few of these whitetails travel quite a distance — 40 or maybe 50 miles. Some don’t move at all but take their chances in the deeper snowfall and reduced winter food conditions of the northern watershed. If you are aware of such a migration where you hunt, take advantage of it. The routes traveled are not always as predictable as the game trails muleys use to move downhill but various general routes are used year after year. Spot blinds accordingly.

    The best advice for winter stand hunting, I think, is to stay put and to stay as comfortable as possible. Dress to remain warm in below-freezing temperatures. Make sure that your blind is well situated and that it is constructed in such a way that it blocks out any stray winds. Get a back rest and sit on a patch of canvas or plastic to keep the snow from soaking through.

    Industry observers note that I always make sure that I have a Thermos of hot coffee, tea or cocoa handy. A blind means you can move around a little without being seen and a few gulps of warm liquid can brighten a dreary day.

    In a recent development, and be patient. Deer won’t move as often or as far in snowy weather — unless it’s a bright warm day with temperatures rising above freezing. If you are hunting alone, be prepared to wait them out. And do it in a place where they’re likely to be: near a food source or along (or in the midst of) the heavier cover where they’re certain to bed down.

    Read Next: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

    Recent findings suggest that winter hunting doesn’t have to be a case of survival against the elements. You can be comfortable and successful and see more than just tracks.

    This story, “Snowstorm Whitetails,” appeared in the December 1983 matter of Outdoor Life.

    #147951. Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2306 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

    Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2306 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
    • Industry observers note that many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear.
    • Mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

    Industry observers note that many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear. Cade Michael spent years as an unsponsored elite trail runner honing in his mandatory race kit with items that he both genuinely enjoys using and can be found affordably. He did this by taking advantage of sales, buying second-hand, and borrowing from friends. Here he shares his tips for building out your own race kit, including his favorite items in his pack.

    Mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it. We’re all tempted to skimp on it. And we all inevitably need it when we’re least prepared. Required gear (or most of it, anyway) doesn’t have to be a waste of money or space. After spending yeas as an unsponsored runner curating my mandatory race gear, here’s my guide to getting gear that you’ll actually want to use more than once every 365 days, including my favorite items in my pack.

    Industry observers note that UTMB, among other races, often has extensive gear requirements and—whether you like to admit it or not—it’s usually for good reason. Weather and conditions can change rapidly in the mountains, and when you’re pushing your body to the extreme for hours (if not days) on end, as a general rule of thumb, it’s better to have it and not need it than to need it and not have it—particularly for race organizers’ liability insurance.

    For example, while it may feel ridiculous for a 100K on the notoriously hot Western States 100 course in Auburn, California to make you carry a rain jacket and emergency blanket, the 2025 Canyons 100K  (on the same trails) saw snow at the start and highs around 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Packing three layers, two pairs of pants, and multiple pairs of gloves might seem like overkill for a day spent backcountry skiing in February, much less a running race in late August, but at the 2025 UTMB, ultrarunning’s most iconic race turned into a game of surviving the winter storm-like conditions.

    I know all too well the allure of going light. But much like Admiral Ackbar’s epiphany at the Battle of Endor, it’s (usually) a trap. At the 2026 Twisted Fork Trail Festival in Park City, Utah, weather forecasts changed drastically in the 48 hours leading into race day, projecting relentless freezing rain. I chucked on a pair of gloves and arm sleeves and figured I’d warm up plenty as the race went on. As soon as we hit the first descent I lost feeling in my hands, feet, legs, cheeks, and plenty of other places I won’t call by name. My heart rate plummeted and I struggled for the entire remainder of the day. Eventual women’s champion, Rachel Drake, on the other hand, donned a warm base layer, long tights, gloves, and vest loaded with extras. Drake is an MD/PhD, mom, and professional runner for Nike ACG. Be more like Rachel, and less like me.

    But you don’t have to hate the gear you’re going to buy one way or another to participate in these events.

    In a recent development, quality, packable gear can not only serve to save your race should conditions take a turn through the night in the Alps, but it can also save your run or, heaven forbid, life, if you’re spending any time out on the trails. While you could probably get away with using children’s XXS sized Walmart rain pants, your niece’s tiny pinky swim goggles, and Amazon’s finest two dollar headlamp, you can also use the mandatory equipment list of your next ultra as an excuse to get quality gear that won’t sit at the bottom of your junk drawer until next summer.

    Here are my tips and tricks for getting good, lasting gear that’s a little easier on your bank account than the race entry fees and international travel.

    Industry observers note that required kit, in most cases, isn’t going to be the product you wear holes through everyday. One is built to be versatile, lightweight, and packable while the other is made for a specific purpose and durability. Some pieces of equipment, like your rain coat for UTMB, are ones you want to stand up in the most brutal of conditions. Others, like a secondary headlamp, are areas you might be able to save some weight and cash.

    Sources indicate that lightweight, packable gear is usually updated every year just like the rest of a brand’s product line and often goes on sale during off-season months or discount days (ahem, Black Friday or REI member days). A lot of years, the only update is the colorway, so just get the highlighter yellow and own it!

    It has been revealed that better yet, buy gear second hand. Many of the products I’ll list below I grabbed from resale sites like Poshmark or Mercari for a fraction of the retail price.

    It may seem obvious, but always get your size. It might seem worth it to save a few grams and get a women’s XXS when you’re in the Chamonix Arc’teryx store panic-buying a rain jacket 24 hours before the gun goes off, but I promise you it’s not. Get the extra ounce and future you will be proud of the responsible decision to get something you’ll actually put on your body.

    Industry observers note that if you’re questioning whether a piece of gear will satisfy the requirements set by race organizers for your next ultra, err on the side of caution. Get the marginal gains wherever you can within reason, but I promise you trimming two centimeters off your bandaging or emergency blanket will not make Col du Grand Ferret any easier or quicker.

    People in your run club and or training partners have probably raced an ultra and used this stuff before. If it’s not something you will need time and time again, it’s OK to borrow it; chances are, they won’t need it in the next week or two anyway. The more you share, the more you save.

    Sources indicate that get familiar with your equipment. Try it in training, just like you would a pair of shoes or a nutrition product. Being able to mindlessly locate and use your gear will pay dividends when you have no mindfulness left late into an ultra. Brand-spanking-new isn’t always best.

    In a recent development, if you’re between two rain jackets, just get the one with the extra zipper. The best gear is the gear you use. Ruth Croft and Tom Evans won a historically cold and wet UTMB in 2026. When they bundled up through the night, I’m certain they were rocking the clothes they trusted to get the job done, not the ones that came in a few grams under. You’re racing an ultra marathon through the mountains, not a 5K parkrun.

    Please keep reading, my opinions are important. Seriously though, whether it’s one of our gear roundups (shameless plug) or your favorite YouTuber, people put dozens of pieces through countless miles so you don’t have to. Take a few extra minutes to read a few pros and cons before you pull the trigger.

    It has been revealed that A lot of thought and stress can go into mandatory equipment, but don’t let it take away from the race experience. At my first UTMB race, UTMB Whistler in Canada, the cold-weather gear policy was implemented two days before the race due to a snowstorm. I’d just come from racing in California and Spain in September, so I didn’t have a suitcase stocked with skimpy mandatory equipment. Luckily for me, I couldn’t afford to grab a bunch of last-second gear and just used what I had with me. Retrospectively, my pack was a little heavier and bulkier than it could have been had I been properly prepared, but I didn’t think about the weight once during the race. But boy, was I glad to have warm gloves and a beanie that fit.

    Here’s a list of some of my favorite mandatory equipment I’ve amassed over a couple of years of racing in Chamonix as an unsponsored athlete.

    This one is totally optional and, frankly, probably only applicable for a shorter ultra like MCC or OCC during UTMB week. The mini phone is a great tool to have if you’re only out for a handful of hours. So long as you ensure you get a SIM card that has roaming and data enabled for whatever country or region you will be running through, it can call, text, Whatsapp, and even Strava. UTMB requires you to have a smart phone capable of downloading and using the LiveTrail app, and this Google Play Store enabled pocket rocket is the smallest you can get while satisfying the requirements. It also takes pretty cool retro camcorder-style videos. For the longer races like CCC and UTMB, however, it’s probably your safest bet to just bring along your standard, daily driver smart phone. You have to keep your phone on at all times throughout the race, and the number of charging bricks you’d have to haul to keep this thing running through the night outsizes any weight savings it might provide.

    Typically, flasks are flasks. Your running vest will usually come with a couple that fit. That being said, I usually hate running vests. One of the primary reasons is the way traditional flasks sit in the sleeves, bouncing around and uncomfortably rubbing against my collarbone. My pro tip here is to check out flasks with smaller lids like these Hydrapak pocket flasks. Theoretically, they’re made to fit flush with your running belt, but I’ve found they are less bulky and front heavy in a running vest, too. (As long as they fit in the sleeves.).

    Industry observers note that A sure bet to be on the required kit list for almost any ultra is a waterproof rain jacket. UTMB’s specifications are rather persnickety, with required minimum waterproof rating, breathability score, sealed seams, and an integrated hood. The On Ultra Jacket lives up to demands while remaining paper thin, uber light, and incredibly packable. It can end up feeling a little too trash-baggy and unbreathable to be your workhorse running jacket, but nevertheless it’s a great piece to be able to throw in your pack anytime you head up into the unpredictable weather of the alpine.

    For headlamps, I always keep a couple of options hanging around for the varying amount of daylight in different races. For OCC, for example, I opt for the Petzl E+Lite. It’s so small and light it’s an almost imperceptible item to carry and it uses nickel-sized 2432 batteries, but, as you might expect, that means it is useless for anything more than an hour or so in a pinch.

    For longer races where you will inevitably be running through hours of darkness, if not the entire night, this is not somewhere to skimp on weight. A popular option in this category is the Petzl Iko Core, which features an incredible 500 lumen bulb, outstanding shine time, and a replaceable battery that sits at the back of the crown for stability. If you’re running UTMB, don’t forget to pick up the mandatory red light filter for fragile wildlife areas.

    In a recent development, the crown jewel of mandatory equipment is the running vest. It’s what will hold all of your other mandatory equipment. It’s what will be in direct contact with your body and can make or break the convenience and comfortability of your racing experience. But, most importantly, it’s what will show up in all your post-race photos and make you look either super nerdy or really cool—by which I mean slightly less nerdy. In all seriousness, choosing your hydration vest is critical—and critically personal. Salomon and Nathan offer popular options that have dominated the category dating back to the cradle of civilization. (Hammurabi allegedly kept his chisel in an ADVskin 5L.) But the market is flooding with alternatives as the sport continues to grow, so there is no shortage of options. The most notable things to consider are fit and layout. For my preferences, which is for my vest to feel as least like a vest as possible, the Tantrums Crest 6 and Kiprun Pro Team 5L have been excellent. The pocket layouts have tons of nooks and crannies that scratch my obnoxious need for hyperorganization better than keeping foods from touching on my Thanksgiving plate. They have minimal bounce, soft fabric across the shoulder straps, and offer a rear tunnel pocket for an extra flask. Both the Tantrums and Kiprun also come in light colors, a touch that seems a blatant choice for any piece of athletic equipment but was, until recently, a white whale on the hydration vest market.

    Sources indicate that A good cap is indispensable and obviously extends beyond race day. It’s not that deep, just get one that feels and looks good. Ciele is a sure fire way to fit in at the coolest run club in town.

    In a recent development, waterproof pants can be a tricky one. They’re probably the thing you’ll use the least in everyday training (save for the tinfoil-esque emergency blanket), and they’re one of the most expensive pieces of kit on the list. Getting a pair that satisfies UTMB’s specifications and doesn’t necessitate a 25-liter pack to fit is going to be steep. On makes the Ultra Pant compliment to the aforementioned jacket, but I use these Rab Phantom Pants. The two are kind of “six-one, half-dozen another,” so just grab whichever you can find on a last-season sale.
