    #147950. Breaking: The Boyhood Deer Hunt That Turned Jim Carmichel Into a Gun Guy

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4521 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: The Boyhood Deer Hunt That Turned Jim Carmichel Into a Gun Guy

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

    ⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that when I was a skinny, major-footed kid in grammar school, I had the unbelievably good luck of being yanked out of school for several days to go on a deer-hunting vacation with my family.
    • Our hosts were old family friends who had struck it rich and bought an historic plantation in Virginia, complete with antebellum mansion and miles of sweet-scented hardwood forest.
    • On the day we arrived, dressed in our Sunday best, in a gleaming pickup truck, our host had shot a nice buck and it hung in the smokehouse.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that when I was a skinny, major-footed kid in grammar school, I had the unbelievably good luck of being yanked out of school for several days to go on a deer-hunting vacation with my family. Nowadays, thanks to the game commission’s deer stocking and management programs, deer are plentiful in the mountains of east Tennessee, but in the 1940s they were nonexistent. That meant that going on a real deer hunt involved traveling hundreds of miles and visiting places as far removed from our farm as was the back side of the moon. It was, to my mind, an elegant adventure, sort of like going to Europe or taking an ocean cruise. Nothing could be finer. My chums were green with envy.

    Our hosts were old family friends who had struck it rich and bought an historic plantation in Virginia, complete with antebellum mansion and miles of sweet-scented hardwood forest.

    On the day we arrived, dressed in our Sunday best, in a gleaming pickup truck, our host had shot a nice buck and it hung in the smokehouse. I remember inspecting the animal in elaborate detail; feeling the texture of its hair, looking at its teeth and bones and, most of all, marveling at the wonder of its gracefully curved antlers.

    It has been revealed that horns, as they grew on cows and bulls, were familiar to me. But antlers were something entirely different — harder, more graceful and certainly more dangerous looking. I nearly lost my senses when told they were shed and regrown every year. For a while I simply didn’t believe it and only gradually allowed myself to be convinced.

    And deer could jump, too, higher than a cow or even a horse. My imagination reeled with stories of these wonderful animals.

    “Come on,” I mentioned, “nothing can jump a high-wire fence.” So my host took me to a crossing place and highlighted where the deer-tracked path led up to a fence then continued on the other side. “Wow, they really can do it. Wait till I tell Mom.”.

    It has been revealed that next day, after breakfast of deer loin, rich gravy and biscuits, I stood in front of the gun rack, itching to get my hands on a genuine deer rifle and go hunting for these wonderful animals. Already, visions of great stags were dancing through my head.

    My dad took the first rifle, a Model 99 Savage in .250 caliber, and my brother selected a shortened .30/40 Krag. Why, I wondered, had he passed over a truly beautiful Model 141 Remington pump-action rifle in .30 Remington in favor of the Krag? Anyway, I liked the pump and was glad I had a chance to use it. But when I was clear of the barn lot and stopped to load the rifle, his motives became clear. Nearly all of the cartridges had a sharp indentation on the primer, meaning they had previously misfired and were now useless. Of the lot, only three had virgin primers, and these I fed into the rifle with the optimism of youth.

    Less than an hour later, I “jumped” a deer literally in his bed. He came up so close to me that for a moment I was so startled I almost turned and ran. He was not the stag of my dreams but he did have antlers, perhaps six points, and he could be mine! At first the buck ran away so fast that it looked as though I wouldn’t have time for a shot, but then he did something that still has me wondering. After running dead away for about 100 yards, he spun around and headed right at me. Clearly, he would pass by within a few feet, and even at full tilt I’d have a fairly easy shot.

    Closer he came and the rifle was at my shoulder, my teeth clinched against the fearful recoil, eye squinted over the sights.

    “There he is, pull the trigger!”.

    Recent findings suggest that “Hurry, he’s getting away. Try another shot!”.

    In a recent development, then the buck whirled again and headed back at me again! He was passing by close enough to hit with a hoe handle.

    According to recent reports, tears streamed down my cheeks. Tears of disappointment, tears of frustration and tears of anger. I’d had a better than fair chance and lost it because of grown-ups who’d palmed off a bunch of useless cartridges on me. On the way back to the house, I tried the last cartridge but like its brethren, it only clicked in dismal failure.

    It started with a deer rifle that wouldn’t fire and a .22 that missed crows, and I’m still at it, studying, asking questions and, bit by bit, unraveling the puzzles.

    As it turned out, I was the only hunter who’d had a “shot” that day, meaning that on the following morning the gun rack was again emptied of all workable deer rifles. All that was left was a little Mossberg Model 151 Rimfire Autoloader complete with a 4X scope (don’t ask how I remember these details, how could I possibly forget?) and several boxes of Super-X ammo.

    In a recent development, the day before, I’d passed a newly disked and seeded field of winter wheat that was covered with crows. Surely they would be there again. “If I can’t shoot a deer, at least I’ll shoot some crows,” I told myself as I lifted the .22 from the rack and pocketed a box of ammo.

    Recent findings suggest that the crows were there, within easy range, but my first shot kicked up dust far to the left and lower than where I’d aimed. When the crows settled back I missed again the same way. Clearly the rifle didn’t hit where the scope aimed. Why? The rest of the day, and the days following, were spent unraveling the mysteries of sight adjustment and bullet trajectory. A whole fresh world of excitement lay before me. So many things to learn about guns and only a lifetime to study them.

    It started with a deer rifle that wouldn’t fire and a .22 that missed crows, and I’m still at it, studying, asking questions and, bit by bit, unraveling the puzzles.

    A small boy can do worse than go deer hunting, even with a rifle that won’t work.

    Every time I look at the 12-point whitetail mounted on my trophy room wall, I wonder if I’d do it over again if I had the chance.

    It was December ’77 and I was after big whitetails on the Guajolota (translates to female turkey) Ranch in deep south Texas. When I say big whitetails, I don’t mean just big, but big-big, Texas-big, the kind of big that makes vaqueros (cowboys) whisper “muy grande” in wide-eyed wonder. The Guajolota is a working cow ranch but, like most big spreads in south Texas, it swarms with quail and so many big-antlered whitetails that owner Jim McAllen got the idea that he could make more money “farming” deer than beef.

    In a recent development, so true to his stock-breeding tradition (McAllen, Texas, is named after Jim’s pioneer family), he set out to make his herd of deer bigger and better by using the same selective breeding techniques proven in the development of superior beef herds. In Texas, just about everyone who hunts deer either owns land, leases hunting rights or hunts on a “pay per day” ranch. (That “per day” arrangement is not the same sort of operation as the exotic game ranches, which also flourish in Texas.) Accordingly, McAllen figured that if he could breed a “super” race of elk-headed whitetails, hunters would just naturally pay more to hunt on the Guajolota.

    The first step in his program was to kill off the “culls” — bucks with skimpy antlers and a tendency to pass on this trait — and save the giant bucks for a while for breeding. The program had been in effect only a few years when I hunted the Guajolota, but signs of its success were abundant on my first morning of hunting.

    Accompanied by my pal Jim Nolen, maker of the well-known Nolen knives and guided by Ed Dutch, who at that time was the ranch’s game biologist but has since become a top wildlife photographer, we hid under a mesquite tree where we could look out over a 60-yard flat of open grassland.

    It has been revealed that with a bit of imagination, you might call the south Texas terrain “brush country,” but it’s not the kind of brush hunting one gets in, say, Pennsylvania or Missouri. Just about everything that grows wild in that part of the Texas empire either sticks, scratches bites or poisons, so stalking deer through the cactus and catclaw isn’t all that much fun. That’s why hunting is usually done from a quick stand or from a high seat that lets you look over the thorny chaparral. Fortunately, there is a high buck-to-doe ratio that makes the bucks especially aggressive and eager to challenge other bucks for available does.

    It has been revealed that the sound of these bucks doing battle is a distinctive clicking and rubbing of antlers that can be heard a pretty fair ways and has the effect of calling other bucks to join the fray. If you ever happen to come upon a couple of bucks fighting it out over some does, you’ll probably spot one or two more waiting their turn, and while the fighting is going on, a smarter-than-average Romeo may be trying to make off with the harem.

    Many years ago, some deer hunters had the clever idea of banging a couple of deer antlers together to imitate the sounds of a fight and thereby call bucks to the gun. It worked like a charm and “rattling” up bucks has become an accepted form of the hunting arts.

    I’ve tried rattling bucks from Maine to California but the only places I’ve had much success were in areas of dense deer population where there were plenty of aggressive bucks. South Texas is the home of rattling, with both the terrain and temperament of the bucks ideally suited for the technique. The trick, though, in addition to knowing how to rattle the antlers together, is finding a stand that gives you a fairly good view of at least an acre or so of relatively open space.

    According to recent reports, some bucks apparently lose all reason at the sound of a fight and dash right in where at any other season they would fear to tread. Some rattlers report having snorting bucks right in their laps after only a moment or two of clicking the antlers. Wiser bucks will come in more cautiously, perhaps circling the stand, wanting to get sight or wind of the combatants. Thus, if you position yourself on the edge of a clearing, you get to see the deer before he gets too close. This also gives the deer a bit of breathing room so he won’t have to get too close and overly spooky. You’ll see deer heads poking out of the bush around the clearing, ears forward, and too curious — or determined — to bound away. More often than not, there’s time for a well-aimed shot, but be sure to keep your rifle close to your shoulder and ready to fire. If they see you move, they’re gone in a flash. Man, deer or fowl, there’s something about poaching on another’s territory that makes any male more than a little spooky.

    In a recent development, greed had slithered to the surface of my consciousness. Greed, unbelievable, unforgiveable greed.

    According to recent reports, I settled back against the forked trunk of the mesquite tree with my rifle resting on my knees. It was a trim little .250/3000 bolt gun stocked by Don Allen and built on a Mauser action that had been shortened a full inch by ace metalsmith Ron Lampert. Nolen, who was to take first turn playing the antlers, was just to my right and Dutch, who wanted some pictures, was a few yards behind, manning a telephoto lens.

    Results were almost immediate. Nolen had banged the antlers no more than twice, twisting and rubbing them together to make the characteristic scrape-click-scrape sound of fighting deer when there, right in front of me, snorting and stomping his feet, was the biggest whitetail buck I’d ever seen on the hoof. He was huge, with perfectly symmetrical antlers. The main beams seemed to grow straight out in a horizontal line before hooking in at the tips. His points stood straight up like rods in an iron gate and the whole picture was a deer-hunter’s fantasy. The buck of a lifetime, too big to be true, perfect. It had to be a lie, a tale told in a deer camp, vividly remembered.

    But he was there, stomping, snorting, beautiful. All I had to do was put the crosshairs on his chest and touch the trigger and my whitetail-hunting days would be over, for never would I see a bigger buck. For long moments, I held the crosshairs on his chest, poised to shoot, listening for the click of Dutch’s camera, Click-click-click it went. Now I had a record of the moment, a deer hunter at the gates of paradise. Every nerve in me howled “pull the trigger, pull the trigger,” but I didn’t.

    Sources indicate that greed had slithered to the surface of my consciousness. Greed, unbelievable, unforgiveable greed. “Look old boy,” it remarked to me, “this is only the first deer. Think about the really substantial ones that are waiting back there in the thicket. We’ve got lots of time to wait for the absolute world beater.”.

    Incredibly, I lowered my rifle, worked the bolt and emptied the chamber. Then, settling the crosshairs back on the buck’s chest, I tickled the trigger.

    “Click,” it went, and the buck was gone.

    “Just wanted to know what it felt like to pull the trigger on a giant buck,” I explained to an absolutely astonished Jim Nolen.

    “Why didn’t you shoot?” Dutch asked.

    “Waiting for something bigger,” I allowed.

    “That’s as big as they get,” was his answer, and I knew greed had done me in.

    That morning we rattled in a couple more trophy-size bucks, but nothing nearly so grand as the first, so I couldn’t bring myself to raise the rifle. That afternoon, after a lunch of chili and frijoles served on a tortilla, cowboy-style, followed by a siesta, we tried again — but the antlers were cold and nothing answered the challenge.

    That evening a few of McAllen’s vaqueros stopped by the bunkhouse for cerveza and conversation. “It is true,” they asked, “you had El Macho Grande in your sights and did not shoot? Why?”.

    I really couldn’t answer, but one thing for sure, if I ever saw him again I would shoot.

    It has been revealed that next day the antlers were still cold, so by midafternoon we changed tactics and climbed into a tower where we could watch for deer crossing a narrow sendero (a rough, clear-cut roadway). The view from the tower allowed us to look down into the endless thicket, but no deer were moving. By early evening I had counted dozens of javelina, the small wild pigs of the Southwest, and had seen more quail than I thought existed, but no deer other than an occasional doe.

    The sun hung low over the deep Texas thicket and a soft haze had wrapped itself around the evening air when the buck stepped into the sendero. The distance was just a bit more than 200 yards, but even with my 7X binoculars, the antlers were hard to judge because the sun was behind the deer, reflecting through the haze so that the deer seemed to be the center of a psychedelic burst of rainbow color. It was not a vision of earth, but a dream in pastel colors with quail calls for background music.

    The buck moved slowly, a step at a time, nibbling shoots of greenery. But his antlers remained a mystery. We could see that they were substantial and exceptionally high, but the way they reflected shafts of gilded light made rational judgment impossible.

    “I can’t see his antlers clearly,” Nolen whispered, “but I can see points everywhere.”.

    Industry observers note that the buck was nearly across the sendero now and in a moment he would be gone, perhaps forever. I’d already let the trophy of a lifetime slip through my fingers. Did I dare risk losing a second chance? My trigger finger tightened and the little rifle spoke gently to the soft evening.

    In a recent development, the buck was a freak, wearing incredible antlers that had grown to typical, though huge, shape on the right side but with an oddly palmated branch on the left. Is it the trophy of a lifetime, a one-of-a-kind specimen never to be duplicated? Or just a freak with outsize antler growth? I wonder. I wonder every time I look at it on the wall.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to liberal season and bag limits, Alabama has some of the biggest-antlered and heaviest-bodied whitetails I’ve ever looked at. One Alabama trophy deer I saw a few years back got me so excited that I spent several consecutive seasons there trying to bring home the granddaddy.

    And I saw lots of bucks, some eight and 10-pointers with such seductive racks that I was often tempted to touch the trigger. Patience prevailed, though, and as days turned to weeks I became more or less accustomed to the sight of the Alabama sun setting over a hardwood thicket in which, from a tree stand, I might be glassing from two to six substantial-antlered bucks at one time. But as I said, I wanted only the he-coon of the hardwoods and nothing else would do.

    How was it, then, that I eventually shot a little eight-pointer?

    According to recent reports, hoping to relieve the tedium of my daily wait-and-watch routine, I got myself invited to a party hunt, and on the appointed morning found myself in the midst of an incredible spectacle. The setting was a beautiful Southern mansion complete with curving driveway and vast, oak-bordered lawns. What made the scene so bizarre was the unbelievable variety of humanity strolling or squatting about the neatly clipped grounds. Tweed shooting jackets and English riding boots mixed with faded overalls and run-down clodhoppers while the elegant accents of aristocratic Southern speech were punctuated with the staccato “patoos” of well-aimed tobacco juice. There had been a violent thunderstorm during the night, and judging by the smells of wet wool and soaked leather, many of the attendees had passed the night in the rain.

    Recent findings suggest that A metal tub about the size of a horse watering trough was being set up on a stone foundation, eventually to be filled with gallons of cooking oil, and nearby a wild-eyed chap was tugging at a heavy chain leash in a futile attempt to separate two snarling dogs. “Get back,” he yelled when I approached to help, “these dogs are killers.”.

    “Then why don’t you leave them alone?” I asked.

    “I’m trying to keep them from killing each other until Significant Bob wakes up.”.

    “Who is Big Bob?” I had to ask.

    “That’s him over yonder,” he responded, waving his free hand in the direction of an inert form stretched out in the tangled remains of what appeared to have once been a rose garden.

    I meant to take a closer look, but at that moment a silence fell over the assembly as a spry black man of uncertain vintage, his hair a fluffy white, came down the brick-paved path leading from the major house.

    It has been revealed that “Mista William is a commin’,” he chanted. “Mista William is commin’, here he come now.”.

    In a recent development, sure enough, there was the great one himself, Mister William, owner of thousands of acres of prime farmland and hardwoods, home to the biggest whitetails to be found anywhere. Obviously, Mister William had reached that unique station in society where elegant or even proper attire was no longer required as an emblem of station or success. Accordingly, he was outfitted in soiled chino work pants and shirt, the tail of the latter flapping loosely about his backside, muddied work shoes with, as I remember, only one sock and crowned off with an ancient straw hat that was liberally ventilated with odd-size holes. Yet there was no denying his regal presence. As he puffed unsteadily along the brick pavement, pausing occasionally to scratch, spit or realign his direction, there was a chorus of salutations and more than a few caps were doffed.

    “Mornin’ Mista William.” “Fine day Bill.” “Good to see you Mista Bill.”.

    Each greeting was received with a wave and every face was recognized by name.

    “Glad to see you, Jack.” “Nice of you to come over, Pete. How’s Mary and the kids?” “Hi Ralph.”.

    When at last he faced me, his eyes narrowed, searching for a name.

    Sources indicate that “Nice to meet you sir. I’m Jim Carmichel and I appreciated the invitation to your deer hunt.”.

    “Glad to have you, glad to have you,” he gestured grandly. “This hunt ain’t much, just something me and the boys like to do every year about this time.

    According to recent reports, “Hey there you, Jake, tell Big Bob I noted to put Mr. Carmichel here on the road where the deer cross.”.

    It has been revealed that with that he ambled back up the walk, mounted the porch steps and turned to face the breathless assembly. “Boys, the hunt’s on.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the next few moments were lost in a bedlam of shouts, cheers, running feet and spinning truck tires. Seated in the back of a pickup (I almost made the fatal mistake of climbing into a truck full of savage curs) that fishtailed out of the driveway in a shower of mud and gravel, I caught a glimpse of Mister William as he turned and re-entered the great house, aided by his white-topped butler. Apparently he was not attending his own hunt.

    Positioned as I was, on a muddied logging road, I could hear the baying pack of Catahoula curs as they topped a ridge nearly a mile away. As the baying grew louder, it was apparent they were coming my way and would cross the road in front of me. Mister William had indeed given me the best stand on the hunt and in just a few moments I would have a shot.

    I was using a borrowed shotgun loaded with No. 000 buckshot and the deer would be crossing from right to left, a dead-easy setup. When the deer broke from cover and bounded across the road, I swung the bead some two feet ahead of his chest and was tightening on the trigger when I realized that it wasn’t much of a buck. An eight-pointer, perhaps, but it was a bucket-head without much width, height, or thickness of beam. The buck certainly wasn’t the world-beater I wanted. With another bound, the young buck disappeared into more timber.

    By then the road was covered by a blanket of howling and snarling beasts with their owner, Big Bob, not far behind.

    Industry observers note that this was the first time I had had a close-up look at Big Bob and he was, to be sure, an awesome apparition. Clad only in bib overalls and a white T-shirt, despite the chill of the day, Big Bob stood a good six or eight inches over six feet and was as wide as a church door. His hair, probably waist length, was knotted behind his head in the style of a samurai warrior, and when he spoke I could see that every tooth in his head was covered in gold. His bout with the rose garden had criss-crossed his arms and face with bloody lacerations, and at his side swung a hunting knife that looked as long as a Saracen scimitar.

    As he strode toward me — eyes wild, face blood-caked and mouth flashing of gold — the sword banged against his knee. It was the only weapon he carried. Considering his size, the obvious strength of his hands and arms and the fierceness of his countenance, the knife was more of an affectation than a necessity.

    “Where’s the deer?” he asked. “I didn’t hear you shoot.”.

    “How come? His tracks is right there in front of you.”.

    “He wasn’t a good trophy,” I answered.

    At this, his eyes narrowed, “Mister, we ain’t huntin’ trophies, we’re huntin’ meat. We got a lot of people to feed tonight and if you don’t shoot somethin’ these dogs get meaner than they already are.” Major Bob made his point very convincingly.

    “The next time something comes by, I’ll be sure to shoot,” I promised.

    According to recent reports, and that’s exactly what I did. A couple of hours later, the howling pack came by again in violent pursuit of a distinctly undistinguished little eight-pointer.

    That evening, my buck and two others that had been killed during the hunt were sliced into bite-size chunks, rolled in batter and deep-fried in the gas-fired horse trough I’d noted earlier.

    Sources indicate that in time, huge platters were stacked with the delicious-smelling venison tidbits but, for some reason, no one took so much as a single bite. This struck me as curious because no one had eaten since breakfast and I assumed that everyone was as famished as I was. Not wanting to violate local custom, I decided it best not to serve myself until someone else had done so.

    Sources indicate that the reason for the holdup was soon apparent, however, when Mister William’s butler appeared and announced the immediate arrival of his benefactor. “Here come Mista William, ever’body git ready, here he come now.”.

    Mister William’s appearance was greatly improved; not only was he better turned out than several hours previous, but his gait was markedly steadier.

    It has been revealed that without a word to the hushed onlookers, he marched straight to the deep-fry trough and extracted a crispy brown morsel of batter-dipped venison. For a moment he chewed thoughtfully, eyes cast heavenward. Then, with a sly smile, he made his pronouncement, “Boys, this meat is fit to eat.”.

    Later, food and drink in hand, I was buttonholed by Significant Bob, his countenance no less ominous than earlier and his face still blood-caked from his personal war of the roses.

    “If you had shot that other deer,” he allowed, “we would have had some extra meat for my dogs. Now I have to feed ’em dry dog food, which makes their bowels tight and they get meaner than ever.”.

    “Here,” I answered, handing him my half-emptied plate, “they can have mine.”.

    This story, “Whitetails I Have Known,” appeared in the September 1982 issue of Outdoor Life.

    Sources indicate that savvy shoppers know Black Friday is the Super Bowl of savings. These days, it’s more like Black Friday Week, which gives us even more time to browse the best deals.

    Sources indicate that for skiers, there’s no better time to refresh your gear closet than November, when you start taking stock of what you own and what you need for the season. The good news is that Evo is a one-stop shop for everything from hard goods to travel bags, and the deals are plentiful. Keep reading to see what the SKI team is recommending from Evo’s major Black Friday sale.

    We’ll admit it’s not the sexiest gift on anyone’s list, but Evo’s Roller Ski Bag is on sale, and it’s a no-brainer for ski travelers who want to bring their own skis and ensure they arrive safely at their destination. The bag has wheels, which is essential for hauling skis through airports and parking lots. It also holds up to two pairs of skis, poles, boots, outerwear, and accessories, all in padded, durable compartments. Internal straps keep everything in place, and the bag folds up for compact storage between trips. —Samantha Berman.

    I’ve long appreciated the Arc’teryx Sentinel for its clean, understated design and thoughtful features. It’s a serious technical shell without a lot of unnecessary bells and whistles, and the weather protection is hard to beat.

    According to recent reports, what I especially like is the longer, freeride-inspired silhouette, which provides plenty of coverage over my hips and works well with bibs. The fit feels streamlined without being restrictive, and I can comfortably wear a lightweight puffy underneath on colder days. When the weather turns, the three-layer GORE-TEX construction and helmet-compatible StormHood help seal out wind and snow.

    Sources indicate that the latest Sentinel has been updated with a tougher 100-denier face fabric, a refined fit, larger hand pockets, and a latest chest pocket. It’s also designed for moving between the resort and backcountry, which is exactly the kind of versatility I look for in a shell.

    The fabric is on the stiffer side, especially when new, and takes a little time to break in. But it isn’t excessively loud or crunchy, and I appreciate that rugged feel in a jacket designed for years of hard use. The Sentinel is a significant investment, so finding one on sale makes it a lot more appealing. —Sierra Shafer.

    It has been revealed that I’m a big fan of getting dressed for skiing in the lodge instead of the parking lot, so I’m usually hauling my skis, boots, and assorted gear from the car. The Yardsale Day Bag makes that whole process a lot easier.

    In a recent development, at 30 liters, it’s roomy enough to fit everything I need without becoming a bottomless black hole. The magnetic closures, internal divider, dedicated pockets, and key ring help keep smaller items organized, while the cinch closure makes it easy to throw in bulkier gear without worrying about things falling out. There’s even a padded laptop sleeve for days when I’m working from the mountain and hoping to sneak in a few lunch laps.

    Recent findings suggest that one of my favorite details is the suitcase sleeve, which lets me slide the bag securely over my rolling carry-on when I travel. No more tote bag constantly slipping off my shoulder or luggage at the airport.

    In a recent development, it’s also plenty durable. I’ve shoved it under countless lodge tables, dragged it around on trips, and even spilled what appears to have been an entire glass of red wine inside it. Most of the evidence came out in the wash, and I still reach for this bag constantly. —SS.

    I’m firmly in the mittens-over-gloves camp. They’re warmer, more comfortable, and I’ve been skiing in Oyuki mittens for years. I’ve worn every pair I’ve owned until the insulation eventually packed out, usually after four or five seasons of heavy use. That kind of longevity has made me a loyal fan.

    In a recent development, the Sencho GORE-TEX mittens combine waterproof protection with warm PrimaLoft insulation and a soft wool lining. What I especially like about OYUKI mittens is how supple and comfortable they feel, without the excessive bulk that can make some mittens frustrating to wear. I can still manage poles, zippers, and most of the little tasks that come up throughout a ski day without constantly taking them off.

    The wrist coverage helps eliminate that annoying gap between your mittens and jacket sleeves, while the leashes mean I can pull them off on the chairlift without worrying about losing one.

    According to recent reports, I also love the brand’s Japanese roots. Oyuki means “big snow,” and the kanji in its logo translates to “smash pow.” How can you not love that? —SS.

    Industry observers note that when I reach for an insulated jacket on a resort ski day, odds are high it’s the Halfdays Georgie puffer. It’s one of the brand’s original styles, and it’s a classic for a reason. The 550-fill body is warm without being bulky, and the 15,000mm waterproof rating keeps you dry all day on a powder day. My favorite features are the pockets, which were clearly designed by people who ski: they’re intuitively placed and even come with a goggle wipe and a phone leash. The snap-removable hood fits over practically every helmet, too. The dark green colorway is currently on sale, and it just so happens to be on my wishlist.

    Evo is also offering a bundle deal for the Georgie Puffer and Alessandra Pants for $644 (down from $920) —Jamie Aranoff.

    The Hydra Thermagraph delivers impressive performance and style for the price, making it one of the better values in women’s ski outerwear—especially at its Black Friday discount. It pairs a waterproof, breathable 20K infiDRY shell with Thermagraph body-mapped insulation that puts warmth where you need it rather than throughout. Add in features including underarm vents, a helmet-compatible hood, a powder skirt, and generous pockets—including a dedicated phone heater pocket—and you’ve got a jacket that can handle everything from frigid chairlift rides to deep powder days. —SB.

    Recent findings suggest that the Stio Pinion Down Hooded Jacket is one of those versatile layers that earns its keep well beyond ski season. Its lightweight, packable design and water-resistant 800-fill HyperDRY down make it an excellent layer under a shell, adding warmth without unnecessary bulk. The clean, casual styling also makes it a solid everyday grab for walking the dog, running errands, or grabbing après beers. It’s a worthwhile Black Friday upgrade for the minimalist on your list who doesn’t like to waste closet space. —SB.

    It has been revealed that I first fell for the Head Kore 94 at SKI Test, and it has quickly become one of my favorites. It carried me through Utah’s unusually warm winter, when I needed a ski that wasn’t afraid of a little ice. On the few powder days we did get, it stayed afloat better than expected, and never felt like it was sinking. It’s a jack of all trades, which is exactly what I want in a daily driver. The 2027 model is out now, but there’s not a huge change from 2026, so snagging these for under $400 is a win. —JA.

    You can read the full review here.

    The Cotopaxi Tasra 16L Backpack hits the sweet spot as a ski-day pack: compact enough to stay out of your way on the lift, but roomy enough to carry the essentials, from an extra layer and snacks to water, sunscreen, and other necessities. Its 16-liter capacity keeps you from overstuffing it, while multiple pockets, dual water-bottle sleeves, and a durable recycled-polyester construction make it a practical choice. —SB.

    Kari Traa makes base layers for the girls who shred. I absolutely love my sets from this brand, founded by an Olympian, and I find that the capri pants never slip down, which is seriously important when it comes to successful layering. These 100-percent merino wool pieces will keep you warm all day, and when you start to sweat, they’ll keep you dry, too. Mix and match patterns for a fun base layer that’ll last for many seasons to come. —JA.

    Industry observers note that I’ve skied almost exclusively in Le Bent socks for years, and the Compression Zero Cushion is a favorite. It took me a while to come around to compression socks, but now I appreciate the supportive fit, especially on long days in ski boots.

    I prefer a really thin ski sock because I like being able to feel my boot, and Le Bent’s blend of merino wool and bamboo-derived rayon does an excellent job managing moisture. There’s a misconception that thicker socks are always warmer, but a thin, moisture-wicking sock helps keep your feet dry, which goes a long way toward keeping them warm. And in a snug ski boot, extra bulk can compromise fit and circulation.

    Recent findings suggest that the compression is noticeable without feeling restrictive, and the socks stay put all day. No sliding, no bunching, no annoying wrinkles inside my boots, even when I’m touring and moving around a lot more than I would on a resort day.

    I also appreciate the height. I have long legs, and these come up high enough to meet my three-quarter-length base layers without leaving an uncomfortable gap of bare skin. They may not technically be on sale at evo this Black Friday, but I’m still taking the reminder to repurchase before ski season starts in earnest.—SS.

    Seven states, two countries, three acupuncturists, and one orthopedist later, a skier with hard-to-fit feet found the bootfitter she needed. (Photo: Courtesy Abigail Barronian).

    Sources indicate that overview: This first-person essay follows one skier’s years-long search for ski boots that fit, with bootfitters in seven states and two countries, a visit to an orthopedist, three acupuncturists, and a stranger’s garage. It’s a funny account of what hard-to-fit feet can drive a person to do, and a reminder that the right bootfitter can change everything.

    Recent findings suggest that in my quest for ski boots that fit, I’ve seen bootfitters in at least seven states and two countries. I’ve visited Evo and REI, small independent shops, local chains, and garages-turned-ski shops. I’ve consulted boot designers, brand reps, professional athletes, and gear reviewers; tried Intuitions, ZipFits, and custom footbeds. I’ve seen one orthopedic doctor, three acupuncturists, and two physical therapists. I’ve stayed up at night thinking about boots, and developed recurring stress dreams about them.

    Last season, I was beginning to consider looping in a tarot reader or astrologer. Maybe I needed a psychotherapist, or a priest. Maybe I’d have to just quit skiing. And then, finally, I found my bootfitter. But not before resorting to some questionable behavior along the way. Here are seven desperate things I did in my search for a bootfitter who could solve my ski boot challenges.

    Sources indicate that every pair of ski boots I wore from ages two through 22 were hand-me-downs from my older brothers. Then I started working in the ski industry. While skiing around Massive Sky during a media event, a kind man working for Nordica looked at my feet with a frown.

    Recent findings suggest that “What are those?” he asked. I was sliding around in some decade-old size 26.5 monstrosities. He shook his head and invited me to swing by the Nordica headquarters in Fresh Hampshire. There, he measured my feet and sent me off with a pair of 25.5 Nordica Promachines.

    It has been revealed that everything changed. Suddenly I was in an aggressive stance, my shins met real resistance, my power transfer improved dramatically. I got a taste of what a good boot can do, shortly before developing a wicked case of tendonitis in my ankles and shins.

    Recent findings suggest that after two seasons of excruciating, day-ending pain, I booked an appointment with an orthopedic foot and ankle specialist. I knew my boots were the culprit, and couldn’t be sure a doctor would understand the whole foot-encased-in-rigid-plastic thing. I lugged a giant bag with both my alpine and touring boots into the orthopedic practice and pulled them out for show-and-tell.

    The physician kindly assured me he knew what ski boots were, and that I wasn’t dealing with any serious medical complications. I’d have to take my boots back where they belonged.

    According to recent reports, the owner of Santa Fe’s one dedicated ski shop sized me down yet again, into the stiffest 24.5 he had on hand—a 110 from Fischer. I felt like I was skiing in socks and a vise-grip at the same time, and I lost feeling in my feet on the first lap. Mercifully, he let me return them.

    It has been revealed that I’d hit the central problem: boots major enough to be comfortable gave me tendonitis, and boots small enough to prevent it gave me bunions and nerve pain. So I took my boots to Taos Bootdoctors, where a whole team of bootfitters worked patiently to expand the forefoot. I’d ski for a day or two and come back, over and over, looking for just a few more millimeters. I brought six-packs and did my best to be charming, and the lovely staff never made me feel less important than the tourists dropping thousands of dollars on gear. Still, I couldn’t finish a day without pain.

    In a recent development, I soldiered through the season, eyeing an upcoming hut trip with dread. I could manage shorter tours, but a week of daylong missions posed some real problems. Once we were in the mountains, I knew no amount of bunion donuts and anti-inflammatories would save me. I had to instate boots-off breaks in the middle of eight-hour ski days, carefully pulling my socked feet out of jail and propping them up on a backpack in the snow while my friends took an extra lap. Sweet, stupid relief.

    It has been revealed that finally, I heard a rumor about a man in Seattle working out of his garage who was willing to do unorthodox things to ski boots. He had a history of custom-fitting plug boots for ski racers, which seemed like a good sign. While visiting family in Washington, I brought him both pairs of boots.

    He looked at my feet, listened patiently, and rattled off a comprehensive proposal that involved several devices I’d never seen before. Overnight, he molded both pairs into a completely new shape. I never had to touch either boot again, and proceeded with great pleasure to ski 12-hour days in the backcountry and endless resort laps with happy feet. I had found him—the bootfitter I was looking for. Then, he retired.

    It has been revealed that when my touring boots started to go, I bought a replacement pair and nobody could make them fit. The experience began to take on mythic proportions. I felt like the princess with a pea beneath her many mattresses, or an ugly stepsister trying to cram her foot into a crystal slipper: all discomfort and wrong fit.

    Recent findings suggest that it seemed my trusty Tecnicas were the problem. I tried on every touring boot at ski shops in three states. I ordered over a dozen pairs online, obsessively double-checking return policies and momentarily racking up a very scary credit card bill. Eventually, I came crawling back to my old Tecnicas with no initiative, two full seasons into the search.

    I hesitated to say yes to ski trips, afraid I’d have to sit out ski days because of pain or busted gear. Eventually, it happened: I took my tired old touring boots to Rogers Pass in B.C. and, on day three, broke the upper cuff clean off the bottom section of the boot. Thankfully we were just a few hundred yards from the truck. I spent the entire day sitting at the trailhead.

    In the meantime, my alpine boots had begun to warp. I found a replacement pair and was back at square one: home in New Mexico, with two pairs of ski boots that didn’t fit, rapidly dwindling patience, and no bootfitter.

    It has been revealed that I considered that this might be the end of the road for me as a skier. Then, I learned that one of the best skiers I know had been contemplating quitting the sport because of foot pain. He’d even gone so far as to teach himself to snowboard. But then he found exactly what I’d been looking for: yet another fit-obsessed industry veteran working out of his garage.

    I visited another home workshop in western Washington and the bootfitter listened carefully as I explained the concern. Then, he overhauled both pairs of boots, tirelessly stretching the forefoots to give my feet room to breathe. They took on a completely new shape: generous and wide. I took both pairs out for a spin and sighed in relief.

    Sources indicate that there are a lot of great bootfitters out there. But for a freak like me, I’ve learned I need something of a mad scientist. If you’re plagued with bone spurs, high insteps, wide feet—there’s hope, I promise. With a little faith, a lot of persistence, and maybe something like divine intervention, I trust you’ll find the bootfitter you need. Let’s just hope they don’t retire.

    #147942. Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1534 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

    Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.
    • Sources indicate that now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica.
    • “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.

    Sources indicate that now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica. Case took on the November 8 challenge in part to prove that the things she did before becoming a mom weren’t behind her. If anything, she could come back and do them even better.

    “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France. “They were criticizing me after I came back for my first race postpartum, telling me that I was selfish to be taking that time to train. So I wanted to go out and really prove to myself and remind myself that I could keep doing big things.”.

    Sources indicate that actually, major is an understatement. Of the eight runners who started the Antarctic Ice Ultra 100 miler on Union Glacier, Case was one of four finishers, and second overall. Her finishing time of 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds, a clip of 10:31 per mile, smashed the former overall course record by five hours. Only Yusheng Ni, a top ultrarunner from China with experience racing in Antarctica, ran faster in a upcoming best-ever mark of 17:02:24.

    Here’s the kicker: Case doesn’t even like running in the cold.

    There’s cold, and then there’s Antarctica cold. The race started at 1 a.m. under a 24-hour sun, with temperatures as low as minus 35 degrees Fahrenheit—roughly 35 degrees colder than a typical kitchen freezer. And with fierce polar winds, no exposed skin is safe.

    “I’m someone who doesn’t like when the house goes below room temperature. My partner and I are constantly having a fight about where we set the thermostat,” Case shared. “So this was going to be a substantial challenge for me. I knew that I wasn’t going to love it. But I’m Canadian. There’s no bad weather, there’s just bad clothing, they say.”.

    Finding the right gear was one of the biggest priorities in Case’s preparation. She reached out to other runners who had completed the Antarctic 100-miler in previous years to glean their insight. One offered an unexpected tip: Apply sunscreen inside of her nostrils, since the sun reflecting off the snow can burn there, too.

    She also worked with The North Face, one of her sponsors, to design a custom shoe specifically for the conditions. Breathability was key: She didn’t want moisture trapped inside the shoe, and the sole needed to remain flexible in extreme temperatures. There was also the matter of laces. Frozen laces—or having to tie them with mittens on—were not an option. The solution was a BOA closure system, which let her tighten the shoes by turning a dial. The design also included an integrated, insulated but breathable gaiter and removable spikes she could screw into the soles if conditions got icy.

    The setup worked better than she could have hoped. Case wore two pairs of socks—a thin liner underneath a wool pair—and didn’t change them once during the entire race.

    According to recent reports, “I just set it and left it,” she stated. “And it was one of the things I was most stressed about, because with hands, you can put on more gloves. You can have hand warmers. But toe warmers don’t work when you’re running. They can’t fit in the shoe. And I knew if my toes were cold, I was just going to be screwed. And they were toasty the whole time.”.

    As for the rest of her clothing, Case had to consider another challenge: her sweat rate.

    According to recent reports, “I’m a heavy sweater. Even in just mild cold temperatures, I sweat a liter an hour, and in warm temperatures up to two liters,” she said. “So I knew that I would be at a pretty significant disadvantage, because when you sweat, your gear gets wet and then you’re screwed.”.

    It has been revealed that her strategy was to dress as lightly as possible through her core while keeping her hands, feet and face warm and protected. In the coldest stretches, she wore winter tights under wind pants, along with a thin base layer, a midlayer, and a shell on top. At some points, she stripped down to a thin base layer and shell.

    “As long as I kept moving, I was fine,” she noted. “But I wouldn’t be able to kind of stop and walk if something went wrong.”.

    Recent findings suggest that she never quite felt warm, and some exposed skin on her face did get frostbitten. But she managed to find moments of equilibrium.

    In a recent development, “I felt comfortable at times. And then other times I feel like I was just constantly on the edge,” she mentioned. “I wasn’t freezing, but I was cold. But as long as my feet were OK and my hands were OK, then I was fine to keep moving.”.

    The temperature wasn’t the only feature of Antarctica that concerned Case. She describes herself as a “mountain goat.” Living in Chamonix, she’s accustomed to steep trails and vert—not the flat, repetitive terrain of Antarctica’s 38-loop course.

    In a recent development, working with her coach, Meghan Roche, she shifted her training toward flatter ground and faster running. The change paid off: during her workouts, Case set personal records at several distances, from the 10K through the marathon.

    “I had a love-hate relationship with it,” she stated of the training. “But the funny thing was that every time I had a training session, I was getting PRs, because I just don’t run on flat ground.”.

    Industry observers note that she also tested her gear in a cryotherapy chamber during a trip to Geneva, Switzerland, spending 20 minutes in temperatures that gradually warmed from minus 148°F to minus 22°F. The goal wasn’t so much to acclimate as to understand what the cold would feel like and test her logistics. The session made her rethink her fueling proposal: Pulling off gloves, unzipping a shell, and drinking from a flask in those conditions would be too cumbersome.

    Sources indicate that instead, her camera operator doubled as her crew, handing her a SIS gel and flask every loop. While most competitors visited the aid tent every lap or two, Case aimed to go ten loops—roughly a marathon—between stops. She had to cut the first stretch short when her balaclava froze into a solid block of ice, but after that she managed three 10-loop stints.

    The aid station offered some reprieve, with ramen noodles, mashed potatoes, shots of maple syrup, and Rice Krispies treats, but even small tasks there got complicated. Taking her gloves off for just 30 seconds to go to the bathroom could mean waiting 20 minutes for her hands to warm up again.

    Industry observers note that “There was not a single minute during this race when I kind of just relaxed and allowed myself to switch off,” she says. “In any other 100, I can usually just kind of push past [discomfort], but there, one tiny mistake could end the race for me.”.

    As Case recovers at home with collagen mask treatments to heal her frostbitten cheeks and nose, her next challenge is already on the calendar: becoming the first woman to complete the Montane Arctic Spine, a 500-kilometer race in February. This time, she’ll be on Nordic skis, pulling a sled and traveling solo, with checkpoints as far as 50 miles apart. She’ll need to melt her own snow, pitch her own tent, and carry out the journey without a crew.

    She hopes Antarctica has prepared her for an even harder task.

    “Sometimes the way to get through a really scary thing is to line up an even scarier thing afterwards,” she mentioned.

    Beyond that, Case is developing a project called “94 Degrees,” a film that will show her running the gamut of conditions from minus 40 degrees Celsius in the Arctic to 54 degrees Celsius at Badwater in California’s Death Valley, a 94-degree Celsius spread. (She’s qualified for Badwater but still needs to apply for an invitation, so that part isn’t yet confirmed.).

    And in the meantime, she’ll continue her work for the U.N. while serving as the President of Free to Run, a non-profit organization that uses sport to empower women and girls in conflict-affected areas. And she’ll soak up all the cuddles she can with Pepper, now 2, while sharing stories of that one time she ran 100 miles in Antarctica. It’s a story that almost sounds like a fairy tale.

    According to recent reports, “I actually brought one of her toys, a penguin rubber ducky, with me on the trip, just as a reminder of her,” Case noted. “And then this penguin came out on the course and actually ran alongside me for part of it. I’ve been showing her photos and videos … but still … it’s all kind of unbelievable.”.

    #147934. UTMB Moves to Wednesday in Major 2027 Schedule Shakeup

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1333 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

    UTMB Moves to Wednesday in Major 2027 Schedule Shakeup

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1333 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the 2027 UTMB week-long festival events will take place on Sunday, August 22 to August 28.
    • Recent findings suggest that there are certain immutable facts in the world of trail running.
    • One of those things will change in 2027, as the world’s most famous trail running race series juggles its long-established order of events, Trail Runner learned from UTMB officials.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the 2027 UTMB week-long festival events will take place on Sunday, August 22 to August 28. The flagship Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) will start on Wednesday, August 25, Trail Runner Chamonix correspondent Doug Mayer confirmed with UTMB officials. This article was written under embargo and has been updated with additional information.

    Recent findings suggest that there are certain immutable facts in the world of trail running. Kilian and Courtney are the Greatest of All Time. A trailhead IPA will always be the best recovery drink. And UTMB week at the end of August in Chamonix, France, culminates with a 108-mile lap around Mont Blanc otherwise known as the eponymous UTMB.

    One of those things will change in 2027, as the world’s most famous trail running race series juggles its long-established order of events, Trail Runner learned from UTMB officials.

    Industry observers note that for the past eight years, the alphabet stew of race acronyms comprising UTMB week started with the epic 300-kilometer PTL at the beginning of the week, followed by MCC (40K), TDS (148K), and YCC (a 5-15K youth event), before the three UTMB World Series Finals races: OCC (57K), CCC (108K) and finally UTMB (174K). A 15K event, ETC, was added in Courmayeur, Italy, in 2022.

    There are three notable changes for next year’s event:.

    It has been revealed that race start times are expected to stay largely the same for the UTMB World Series Final races. Start times for other races will be forthcoming shortly.

    According to recent reports, two blazing hot meteors of the global sports world are colliding head on. The International Cycling Union (UCI) Cycling World Championships are taking place in France’s Haute Savoie region—which includes Chamonix. The dates? August 24 to September 5.

    And one date looms particularly large: Sunday, August 29, when the UCI elite men’s road race is scheduled to take place in the towns of Sallanches and Domancy, just a handful of kilometers from Chamonix.

    After the UCI announced the dates for the world championships, President of the French Cycling Federation Michel Callot suggested that UTMB shift its dates.

    Recent findings suggest that UTMB couldn’t move into September, as the Mont Blanc Tunnel that connects Chamonix with Courmayeur, Italy, is tentatively slated to be closed again for maintenance starting on Monday, August 30. The tunnel is critical to the infrastructure of the race series—in fact, it was the reopening of the tunnel in March, 2002, after a tragic fire that forced a nearly three-year closure, that allowed race organizers to host the first edition of UTMB a year later.

    Earlier dates presented their own challenges, too. “We would have been right in the middle of the tourist season,” Isabelle Viseux-Poletti, director of UTMB Mont-Blanc, tells Trail Runner. “In terms of visitor numbers and the number of people using the trails, that simply wouldn’t have worked. Everyone around the table agreed on that point.”.

    It has been revealed that the discussions around the 2027 UTMB Mont-Blanc dates involved official representatives of the prefecture and of municipalities along the races’ courses, notably Chamonix, with its newly introduced mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, and directors of the UCI Championships. In the end, they went with the most reasonable option: juggling the flow of the events to better accommodate the regional impacts, and shifting UTMB week a day earlier to avoid a literal collision of events on Sunday, August 29.

    Industry observers note that the 2027 schedule was developed in close coordination with the office of Chamonix Mayor François Xavier Laffin. Laffin, who himself raced UTMB in 2007, came into office this past spring promising to review UTMB’s relationship with the town, with an eye towards mitigating the growing impacts of the race on the local population and the valley’s fragile alpine ecosystem.

    Those two sporting event meteors have been heading towards a collision for more than a year now.

    This will be the first time the UCI is holding a world championship that brings together all of its disciplines in the same place. That includes 20 events ranging from road cycling to mountain biking, para-cycling, and BMX. The overlap with UTMB in a region about the size of Rhode Island triggered a range of concerns about transportation, safety, and accommodations.

    From the very beginning, the UCI worked jointly with UTMB. “We’ve been discussing this for quite a long time,” Viseux-Poletti claims. ”From the outset, we’ve been working collaboratively to find solutions.”.

    According to recent reports, but coordinating two significant sporting events is about much more than just aligning the dates, and UTMB officials had to wait until the UCI could share details about its needs, too. “In particular, we needed to understand their requirements regarding road access and law enforcement,” Viseux-Poletti indicates. Predictably, some of those decisions took months. And so, it was only in the last several months that coordinating decisions between the entities began in earnest.

    Keith Byrne is one person who has watched UTMB race week play out for the last 11 years. An announcer for UTMB English broadcast, he’s taking the calendar shift in stride. “It’s pretty much going to be business as usual for us just with different days of the week,” he says.

    Overall, Byrne is hopeful about the changes: “Out of some disturbance and adversity, there’s an opportunity to move forward.” He does wonder if there will be fewer spectators out on the course during CCC and UTMB. “Wednesday and Thursday might not be the most productive days in the office,” he joked. “Because we’re going to make sure they have great live coverage to watch!”.

    American Emily Schmitz placed third at UTMB this last year. A year-round Chamonix resident for the past four years, she’s not particularly concerned about lower numbers of spectators out on the course. “There were so many spectators this year. Even if there are fewer, there are still going to be a lot of people out there cheering for you,” she observed. “And, regardless, you’re really focused on your race when you’re out there.”.

    If there’s a race winner among these changes, Byrne thinks it’s going to be OCC. And that’s just fine with him. “OCC will have way more eyes on it, falling on a Saturday. That’s great news for OCC runners.” The race has had fierce competition in recent years, with this year’s race featuring a remarkable duel among the top two women, Lauren Gregory (U.S.) and Naomi Lang (U.K.), who finished three seconds apart. “It was the first time in UTMB week history that the women’s finish got more people watching than the men’s finish,” Byrne noted.

    For spectators, Byrne found the silver lining. “If you’re a trail running fan and a cycling fan, this year you’ll have two events for the price of one.”.

    Recent findings suggest that could this schedule change-up, which further draws attention to the marquee events of the week, be a harbinger of things to come? UTMB officials are offering no clues.

    In a recent development, it is clear, however, that juggling the schedule of UTMB’s many races opens a Pandora’s box of coordination headaches. There are three countries with whom to deal, plus regional authorities, nearly two dozen towns, and multiple public and private rescue services. Even for onlookers, it’s migraine-inducing.

    Sources indicate that UTMB officials declined to comment about whether this upcoming schedule will remain the same in 2028. But they did say more changes are coming. Soon after the 2026 UTMB World Series Finals ended, UTMB officials and the Chamonix’s Mayor’s office began a series of meetings to address areas of concern raised by the mayor. Both parties have promised changes to address concerns. Viseux-Poletti expects the race series and the mayor’s office to jointly announce the news in about a month.

    Doug Mayer is the author of The Race that Changed Running: The Inside Story of UTMB. He lives in Chamonix, France, and is the founder of the trail running tour tech giant Run the Alps.

    Controversial Senate Bill Would Speed Up Development on Public Lands

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On November 19, the United State Senate passed a sweeping 400-page bill with big implications for America’s federally managed public lands.
    • According to recent reports, co-sponsored by Sen.
    • Sources indicate that A large portion of the bill aims to reform or streamline the permitting process that developers must adhere to when applying for projects on federal public lands.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On November 19, the United State Senate passed a sweeping 400-page bill with big implications for America’s federally managed public lands. Called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—or BAAJA for short—the bill would ease permitting restrictions for all sorts of public-land development projects, from mining and drilling to large-scale solar farms and geothermal power projects. Supporters say it would open the door for more clean-energy projects on public lands while reducing utility costs for American consumers.

    According to recent reports, co-sponsored by Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-NM) and Sen. Mike Lee (R-UT), BAAJA has drawn widespread criticism from conservationists, environmentalists, and public land advocates, with groups from the Wilderness Society to the National Wildlife Federation speaking out in opposition. According to the National Council of American Indians, it has also caused serious concerns in tribal nations across the country.

    Sources indicate that A large portion of the bill aims to reform or streamline the permitting process that developers must adhere to when applying for projects on federal public lands. It would do so by shrinking the scope, timelines, and legal challenges currently available under both the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the Clean Water Act (CWA).

    In an October blog post, the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership (TRCP) mentioned “permitting reform rules decide how a pipeline, transmission line, mine or dam gets approved, whether hunters and anglers have any say in where it goes—and what happens to elk winter range, trout streams or migration corridors in their path.”.

    Recent findings suggest that while TRCP has stopped short of publicly opposing the bill, they did highlight several concerns in the post. For starters, they flagged a provision in the bill—Section 1401—that “would make it much more challenging to fix problems once a project is permitted.”.

    Titled “Project Certainty,” this section of the BAAJA bill would restrict federal agencies—like the Bureau of Land Management or the US Forest Service—from revoking previously issued permits during future presidential administrations. Critics say this section of the bill could lock in controversial projects—like a proposed copper-sulfide mine on the edge of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or the 211-mile Ambler mining road that the Department of the Interior (DOI) is pushing for Alaska’s Brooks Range.

    Industry observers note that in a separate blog post, Backcountry Hunters & Anglers (BHA) highlighted similar concerns with the “Project Certainty” provision in the BAAJA bill. “For BHA, this raises questions about whether federal land managers would retain sufficient flexibility to respond to changing conditions and protect public resources over the long term,” the BHA post states. “For example, if a mining project near Minnesota’s Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness received federal approval, these provisions could limit a future administration’s ability to revisit that approval in response to newly identified impacts on water quality or fisheries, depending on the circumstances and applicable legal exceptions.”.

    Aaron Kindle is the Director of Sporting Advocacy at the National Wildlife Federation (NWF). He tells Field & Stream that NWF opposes the BAAJA bill in its current form because it raises too many questions, is moving too fast without adequate public awareness, and it undermines key public-land safeguards.

    Industry observers note that “This is a hugely consequential bill happening during a lame-duck session with very little public understanding,” Kindle says. “[NWF] is pro-permitting reform. But when we do the analysis on this, and we talk to other conservation friends and partners, it’s just too fraught.”.

    Recent findings suggest that kindle says NWF shares both BHA’s and TRCP’s concerns around the bill’s project certainty guarantees for developers. “It shortens review timelines, it narrows what triggers a review, and it kind of locks it in once it’s done,” he says. “We’ve always wanted to be able to do adaptive management on anything that’s done. Anytime you narrow environmental review parameters like this, or make permits too concrete, that’s concerning for a broad swath of our most cherished public lands and waters.”.

    Kindle indicates NWF is also worried that the bill could expedite data center construction on public lands. Up until now, no data center has been permitted on any federal public lands, though the DOI did attempt to approve one on BLM lands in Nevada back in August, before a federal appeals court revoked the permit.

    In a recent development, “What we’ve understood so far is that [BAAJA] shields [data center developers] from future regulations and makes it hard, or maybe even impossible, to revoke the permits once they’ve been awarded,” he adds. “What if we learn at some future point that these things are incredibly harmful to water, air, wildlife, the grid, who knows—and then they’re just locked in place, and there’s nothing we can do about it?”.

    It has been revealed that the Wilderness Society has been one of the most vocal opponents of the BAAJA bill since it first started making headlines in early November. Wilderness Society President, Tracy Stone-Manning, who ran the BLM during the Biden Administration, calls the bill alarming.

    Industry observers note that “Some of the places that hang in the balance are the Boundary Waters in northern Minnesota and the Brooks Range of Alaska, because of the proposed Ambler Road and Arctic Mine, the entire Alaskan Arctic really, and all of that caribou habitat,” Stone-Manning tells F&S. “You’ve also got places in the Lower 48, like the Roan Plateau in Colorado with its amazing mule deer and elk herds, which sportsmen and women fought so hard to protect, and the headwaters of Montana’s Bitterroot River, where they want to build a rare-earth mine up on Sheep Creek. Whatever the Trump Administration decides to do in these places in the next two years, that gets locked in if this bill passes. We won’t be able to undo it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Wilderness Society supports expanded permitting for renewable energy projects on public lands, which have declined steeply during the first two years of the Trump Administration. But for Stone-Manning, the risks of the BAAJA bill far outweigh the rewards.

    Recent findings suggest that “The bottom line is, this bill takes away environmental safeguards for habitat and gives developers certainty,” she says. “Those two things coupled together spell disaster for our country’s conservation heritage and for our public-land hunting and fishing traditions.”.

    Recent findings suggest that many conservationists who opposes BAAJA are confused by Sen. Martin Heinrich’s staunch support for the bill. Heinrich has been one of the Senate’s most stalwart defenders of public lands for years. He has helped secure Wilderness Area and National Monument status for thousands of acres of public lands in his home state of New Mexico, for example. More recently, he was a vocal and outspoken opponent of an attempt to sell off more than 3.4 million acres of Western public lands in the “One Big Beautiful Bill.”.

    Recent findings suggest that today, he’s defending BAAJA in the halls of Congress and in the op-ed pages of major news outlets like the Fresh York Times and the Economist. In a recent interview with Field & Stream, Heinrich cited an urgent need to slow climate change as his primary motivator for helping craft and co-sponsoring the legislation.

    Industry observers note that “This will allow us to put green energy on the grid at a scale where we might be able to mitigate the worst future outcomes of climate change,” Heinrich indicates. “I’ve realized that I’m watching the world change at such a pace, that if we don’t get to work on this, I don’t know what kind of world my grandkids are going to inherit. The places that I fish in New Mexico, for example, are changing. We don’t have a lot of water. If these places go away, and we don’t have snowpack, we’re done. It’s game over.”.

    Industry observers note that heinrich claims the bill address climate change by putting public land renewable projects—like wind, solar, and geothermal—on equal footing with oil, gas, and mining. “We want to bring renewables into the same regulatory permitting regime that the fossil fuel projects already have,” he says. “Right now, oil and gas in particular, and natural gas pipelines, have a sort of privileged position.”.

    According to recent reports, heinrich disputes claims from his critics that the bill weakens key public-land safeguards like NEPA and the Clean Water Act. And he says it won’t expedite or lock-in mining permits in the Boundary Waters.

    “We don’t change or lower standards in this bill; we streamline the process,” he claims. “If you’re a mine developer, you still have to get your Clean Water Act permit, and it doesn’t change the standard for that. When you look at the Boundary Waters, what I don’t see is that project being able to clear is a state Clean Water Act permit, because I just don’t think it will be possible to do mining with open-air tailings at that site—having seen it with my own eyes—without the acid generated making it into the water next door.”.

    Heinrich also disagrees with BAAJA opponents who say the bill will open the door for data center development on public lands. “I don’t think that data centers belong on public lands, and I think any effort to build them on public lands is probably a legal stretch of existing authorizations and presidential authorities,” he adds. “This bill just makes data centers pay their fair freight for attaching to the grid, instead of passing that cost on to everyday consumers in the form higher electricity rates.”.

    The Trump Administration’s current policy around data centers is murky at best. But recent reporting from the Washington Sun revealed that the BLM was reviewing at least 12 data center proposals spread across 17,600 acres of public land in six western states. In its recent strategic strategy, DOI, which manages close to 500 million acres of public land, listed data center development as a top priority, alongside the potential transfer or sale of federal public lands to states and local governments.

    Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) tried to attach an amendment to the bill that would have banned the construction of data centers on public lands altogether when the Senate was debating BAAJA earlier this month. That effort ultimately failed and Wyden voted against the bill, though it still passed the full Senate on 63-33 vote.

    President Trump endorsed the bill in a recent Truth Social post and noted he’ll sign it if it comes across his desk, calling it a massive win for energy independence and dominance. Now its awaiting a vote in the US House of Representatives. House members could vote as early as next week, when they return from Thanksgiving recess.
