    Breaking: 10 Ski Run Drop-Ins That Require Serious Nerve

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every expert skier knows this feeling: You’re standing at the top of a run, skis pointed downhill, looking over an entrance that suddenly seems a whole lot steeper than it did from the lift.
    • Whatever the obstacle, some ski runs are intimidating before you even make your first turn.
    • It has been revealed that *Conditions and snow depth greatly affect how skiable the following runs are at any given time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Photo: Courtesy of Jackson Hole).

    Every expert skier knows this feeling: You’re standing at the top of a run, skis pointed downhill, looking over an entrance that suddenly seems a whole lot steeper than it did from the lift. Maybe there’s a cornice to negotiate, a narrow rock-lined chute to squeeze through, or a cliff that requires a leap of faith. The remainder of the run beyond the drop-in might be flat, for all you know, but getting to it is the challenge of the day.

    Whatever the obstacle, some ski runs are intimidating before you even make your first turn. From legendary substantial-mountain lines to tight, technical chutes, these 10 North American drop-ins are guaranteed to get your heart pumping. Consider them inspiration for the season ahead—or a reminder that sometimes it’s perfectly fine to admire the view from above.

    It has been revealed that *Conditions and snow depth greatly affect how skiable the following runs are at any given time. Check trail status and heed all warnings and closures before dropping in.

    It’s hard to make a list like this without kicking it off with Corbet’s. Perhaps the most famous—and most photographed—ski entrance in North America, this Jackson Hole icon requires skiers to negotiate a rocky cornice before dropping roughly 10 to 20 feet into a narrow, steep couloir. The landing can be soft powder or unforgiving hardpack, depending on conditions, and there’s often a crowd gathered above to watch the action. No pressure. There’s even an entire event dedicated to how stylish—or catastrophic—skiers navigate this tricky entrance.

    Industry observers note that think Corbet’s is intimidating? Meet its even scarierl next-door neighbor. Located just skier’s left of Corbet’s, S&S features a mandatory cliff drop of up to 25 feet, followed by a tight landing and a narrow couloir. Skiers need to make a midair adjustment to line up the landing, leaving little room for error. This one is strictly for the seriously experienced.

    Recent findings suggest that the name doesn’t undersell it. Substantial Sky’s legendary Big Couloir begins with an exposed, rocky entrance that can involve negotiating a cornice before dropping into a narrow, sustained chute. With pitches approaching 50 degrees and a 1,400-foot descent below, it’s a serious commitment from the first turn. Access is controlled by ski patrol, and skiers must check in and carry avalanche safety equipment.

    Alyeska doesn’t do subtle when it comes to steep terrain, and Christmas Chute is a perfect example. The entrance funnels skiers between imposing rock walls before opening into a steep, confined chute. The line averages roughly 45 degrees and drops about 1,500 vertical feet. It’s an intimidating entrance in a spectacularly Alaskan setting, where the mountains are massive and the consequences are real.

    Even the name is enough to make you think twice. The Coffin is a notorious narrow passage in Whistler’s alpine terrain, where skiers squeeze through a tight, rock-lined opening before dropping into the terrain below. Visible from the Peak Chair—but not officially on the trail map—it’s also a popular spectator attraction. The confined entrance leaves little room to get comfortable, making the moment you drop in particularly memorable.

    Palisades Tahoe has no shortage of intimidating terrain, but McConkey’s is among its signature tests of nerve. This steep, rocky feature demands commitment from the entrance, with exposed terrain and little margin for error. The line’s reputation is part of what makes it so compelling: Even accomplished skiers may take a long look before deciding whether today’s the day.

    Industry observers note that not every intimidating entrance involves a giant cliff or mandatory air. Sometimes it’s what you can’t see that gets the adrenaline going. Lobotomy, located off of Silver King peak, in Crystal’s sidecounty zone, is known for its blind entrance and consequential no-fall-zone skiing. You can’t simply peer over the edge and map out every turn before committing. It’s a different kind of mental challenge, and one that earns this line a spot on the list. Note that this is technically hike-to terrain, so come prepared with all the necessary equipment.

    According to recent reports, snowbird is for its steep skiing, and Pipeline Couloir is one of its more intimidating challenges. Getting there requires a hike, but the real test begins when skiers reach the entrance: a steep, rocky drop-in that demands solid technical skills before the couloir even opens up. It’s a reminder that sometimes the most intimidating part of a big-mountain line isn’t the descent itself, but getting those first few turns just right.

    Industry observers note that revelstoke is a playground for skiers who like their terrain steep, deep, and a little intimidating. With a technical entrance and steep, demanding terrain, Discipline rewards, well, discipline and confident, precise skiing. Depending on conditions, the entrance can feature a cornice that adds another layer of commitment.

    Sources indicate that the East Coast gets in on the fun with this Mad River Glen adventure. Paradise is an all-natural trail that starts with a steep drop-in before winding through tight trees, bumps, and rugged New England terrain. There’s no wide-open groomed runway here, and the entrance sets the tone for all that follows. Paradise offers a totally different vibe than all the others on this list, but it’s no less intimidating for those who dare.

    • According to recent reports, the Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ryan Cochran-Siegle at Copper Media Days on November 18, 2026 at Copper Mountain Resort in Copper Mountain, Colorado. Photo: @dustinsatloff // @usskiteam (Photo: Dustin Satloff).

    It has been revealed that world Cup skiing returns to Colorado this weekend as Copper Mountain hosts the Stifel Copper Cup for two days of high-speed competition. For American fans, it’s a chance to cheer on the U.S. Ski Team on familiar terrain—and to see how the country’s top male skiers stack up against a formidable international field.

    According to recent reports, the Nov. 28-29 event features men’s super-G on Saturday and giant slalom on Sunday. Saturday’s race is particularly noteworthy: It marks the first men’s speed race of the 2026-’27 World Cup season and the first domestic men’s World Cup stop of the winter.

    And while the international field is loaded with star power, including Swiss superstar Marco Odermatt, there are several Americans worth keeping an eye on this weekend.

    The headliner for the American men is Vermont native Ryan Cochran-Siegle, a two-time Olympic silver medalist in super-G and one of the country’s most accomplished speed specialists. He’ll make his season debut Saturday in a discipline where he’s proven he can hang with the very best.

    Cochran-Siegle earned silver in super-G at the 2022 Beijing Olympics and added another silver in the team combined at the 2026 Milan Cortina Winter Games. He’s also a former World Cup super-G winner, and his combination of technical prowess and comfort at high speeds makes him America’s best shot at a podium on Saturday.

    It’s worth noting that Copper’s super-G marks the first men’s speed race of the season, meaning everyone is starting from scratch in the discipline. Cochran-Siegle will have the home-country crowd behind him as he takes on a field led by Odermatt and reigning Olympic super-G champion Franjo von Allmen, both of Switzerland.

    For Colorado ski fans, River Radamus’ name always elicits excitement. The Edwards native grew up skiing at Vail, where his parents were ski coaches, and has become one of the most consistent American giant slalom racers on the World Cup circuit.

    Sources indicate that radamus, known for his aggressive skiing style, has developed into a regular World Cup points scorer and a legitimate contender when the course suits his strengths. He’s also familiar with Copper’s terrain from years of training at the resort.

    Sunday’s giant slalom will be a particularly tough test, with Brazil’s Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, the reigning Olympic GS champion and Crystal Globe winner, leading the field. Odermatt and Switzerland’s Loïc Meillard are also contenders to watch.

    Industry observers note that another Colorado connection is Kyle Negomir, a Littleton native and Ski & Snowboard Club Vail product who represents the next wave of American men’s racing. Negomir competes in the technical and speed disciplines and has been working to establish himself as a consistent World Cup presence.

    With the American men looking to build depth behind established veterans like Cochran-Siegle, Negomir is one to watch as the season progresses. A strong showing on home snow would be a big step forward.

    Both men’s races stream live on Peacock and NBCSN. Saturday’s super-G coverage begins at 1:45 p.m. ET, and Sunday’s giant slalom starts at noon ET, with the second run at 3 p.m. ET. Spectators can watch in person; general admission is free.

    #147918. How to Crew an Ultramarathon Like a Pro

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2166 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Crew an Ultramarathon Like a Pro

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
    • Addison Smith is an ultrarunning coach at CTS, one of the most popular and accomplished coaching organizations in endurance sports.
    • It has been revealed that crewing a runner at a trail race may seem like a simple task and, in a lot of ways, it is.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

    Addison Smith is an ultrarunning coach at CTS, one of the most popular and accomplished coaching organizations in endurance sports. He’s headed up the CTS team’s crewing logistics and efforts for races like the Western States 100 and Leadville 100 for years, helping athletes land multiple podium finishes, course records, and Golden Tickets.

    It has been revealed that crewing a runner at a trail race may seem like a simple task and, in a lot of ways, it is. But in the thick of the moment, it can also be stressful, chaotic, and leave you feeling powerless in a situation you hadn’t prepared for. I’ve crewed at a wide variety of trail and ultra races for both cutoff chasers and elite athletes alike. For the past four years, I’ve led the Carmichael Training Systems (CTS) crewing operations for our team crewing efforts at the Western States 100, Javelina 100, Leadville 100, and Canyons Endurance Events. Each race has its own flavor of support, from the rules on the type of assistance you can give, to how frequently you can assist, and how many members each crew can have.

    Ultrarunning really is a team sport, and the proficiency of the crew can be the difference between winning or losing, finishing or DNFing. I’ve seen crew talk a discouraged and fatigued but physically healthy athlete into quitting because they weren’t confident in how to help them through their low patch. I’ve also seen a well-treated blister and some words of encouragement get an athlete back on their pacing plan after a few miles of spiraled thoughts and painful steps.

    The following is a framework for streamlining the crewing process. It’s less a gear guide on what’s in my blister kit and the type of power bank I like using, and more about preparing you to organize and ask the right questions so you can crew with confidence when your runner is depending on you.

    Crewing is a selfless act of caring for a runner. But, paradoxically, it requires a deliberate effort of self-care by the members of the crew as well. For anyone who has crewed a race that lasts most of the day—if not multiple days—you know just how mentally and physically fatiguing an endeavor it can be. You may not be physically running the race, but you’re trying to juggle logistical details—often sleep deprived and outside in harsh conditions. With so many moving pieces, crew members often forget to drink or eat enough themselves—which can show up in the way they communicate or execute their role. Remember that, although some of the tips and tasks outlined below can be time-consuming, the additional organization will hopefully relieve stress, save time, and improve not only your availability for your athlete, but also your enjoyment of the crewing experience.

    Sources indicate that crews of various sizes can be successful. In general, three people is ideal in most scenarios for efficiency and effectiveness. The first crew member can focus on restocking fuel, hydration, and equipment. The second crew member can focus on tending to the athlete directly. They will be the main communicator; giving advice and reassurance, while also tending to their immediate physical needs like cooling or blisters. The third crew member is the pacer. Their primary job is preparing themselves for the long stretch of miles they will run with the athlete by taking care of themselves throughout the day, resting, fueling, and saving energy before their run.

    Specific races would certainly require more crew. For example, the Badwater 135 is a great example of a race where four crew members would be ideal. Crew vehicles are required to follow each athlete along the course, and crews are allowed to pace athletes after Stovepipe Wells (Mile 42). If two people are tasked with driving and pacing, having another crew member ready to cool the athlete and swap bottles every few miles keeps the frequent need for crewing in the hot temperatures efficient. Not to mention having a fourth crew member to fill in and take turns allows crew members to rest and stay fresh in a race that typically takes more than 35 hours to complete.

    According to recent reports, while three to four person crews are ideal, they may not be a possibility for some athletes. I know many couples who crew their significant other by themselves in 100 mile races—often to great success. If you find yourself in a single-person crew situation, most races have a multitude of helpful volunteers at aid stations that can assist you in crewing when needed. Three to four prepared crew members may give the best chance to be as efficient through an aid station as possible, but it certainly isn’t an absolute necessity for success.

    It has been revealed that I would define crewing as people meeting an athlete at aid stations during a race to give physical and emotional support to help them accomplish their race goals. The distinction between physical and emotional support provides the general framework I use to prepare to crew effectively. The physical support could be boiled down to efficient problem solving and transitions, and the emotional side of things to empowering interactions (or a psychological pick-me-up). As crew members, we have an opportunity to give physical support (fueling, hydration, gear, cooling, etc.), as well as emotional support (acknowledgement, guidance, tone, motivation, etc.). You can be incredibly organized as a crew, but if you give the wrong emotional support, it could affect your athlete’s race just as much—if not more—than not being prepared with the proper equipment or nutrition. You need to be prepared for both sides of the crewing process to give both yourself and your athlete the best experience possible.

    Below, I’ll break down my guidelines to being both physically and emotionally supportive for your athlete.

    In a recent development, though this might seem like the most straightforward tip, it’s the one that requires the most planning beforehand. When crewing, you need to prepare  by having the right tools and gear for a variety of situations your athlete might find themselves in–whether that’s dealing with heat, high altitude, an upset stomach, blisters, heat, cold, or any number of other concerns. Here’s a checklist of essential gear that CTS coaching uses at the majority of trail and ultra races we crew:.

    Going into the race, it’s crucial to know how your athlete’s preparation went in the lead-up, what their goals are for the race, as well as their pacing, fueling, hydration, and gear strategies. Once the race starts, it’s equally important to collect real-time information via timing splits or from other crew members. This information gives you a clearer picture of how the race is going, and helps you anticipate what might be needed at the next crewing opportunity.

    It has been revealed that below is what we refer to as an “athlete tracking card”. It is an easy-to-use document that summarizes the necessary context of crewing, so when it’s 2 a.m. and you can’t juggle all of the information needed, you’re still able to reorient yourself around the most crucial details. Whether you’re a first time crew member or an experienced one, I strongly recommend creating your own version of this card to correctly orient yourself around the critical contextual information for the specific athlete and race demands.

    According to recent reports, the last piece to successful physical crewing is effective communication between crew members. Sometimes crewing is a one-person job, but that usually isn’t the case. Ultras often require multiple people to handle various tasks like driving, pacing, cooling, nutrition, etc. The more you can delegate roles–and stick to those roles–the more efficient you can be getting an athlete in and out of the aid station. Once a role has been assigned within the group, it’s up to that person to own their role. In other words, each person should know what gear they need. For example, the person in charge of cooling should know where the bucket, water, and ice are. Each person should also take the initiative to ask the athlete ahead of time how they want the task performed. If you’re in charge of bottles, nutrition, or an athlete’s pack, you should know exactly where they want each item. Owning your role also allows for a more efficient and less stressful pivot if something goes awry.

    In all of my experience at races watching athlete and crew scenarios play out, this is the aspect of crewing that is most easily mishandled. Let’s dive into a race scenario:.

    Sources indicate that you’re racing the Leadville 100 and the second summit of Hope Pass is in your rearview mirror. You’ve been at 10,000 feet or more for most of the day, you’re tired, under-fueled, slightly dehydrated, and you’ve rallied through some stomach concerns. The sun is finally starting to go down and the temperatures are dropping. Your muscles ache and you’re starting to get a hot spot on your foot, but you’re still moving fairly well just behind your goal pace. You can’t wait to get to the Twin Lakes inbound aid station to see your crew, and you’re excited to pick up your pacer. When you get to the aid station, your crew waves you into your tent. You tell them you haven’t been able to get food down consistently, you’re developing hot spots, you don’t want to take in gels anymore, and the planned electrolyte mix sounds terrible now. You ask what you should try. The crew turns to each other, perplexed, saying, “This wasn’t in the strategy, what do we do now?” For the next five minutes, the crew peppers you with a dozen different options you could try. “Maybe change your shoes,” one crew member states. Another chimes in “maybe just change your socks or try those ‘toe condoms,’ I read that they work great.” Instead of one clear solution, you’re given a dozen half-baked ideas for each ailment, and with each passing minute the tone is getting sharper between the crew members, realizing they were supposed to get you out of the aid station minutes ago. You finally make a decision on what hydration and fueling options you’re pivoting to, and decide to change your socks and get out of the aid station. While your crew got you some fresh equipment and nutrition, you’ve also picked up some newfound anxiety and uncertainty.

    In a recent development, bottom line: Crew with calm confidence. If you’re prepared to pivot, there’s less to do on the fly. And when you don’t have a good answer to a mild medical problem, have someone calmly but efficiently go over to the medical staff or aid station captain to ask for advice.

    Acting as a positive light to a runner who likely has experienced a full spectrum of emotions throughout an ultra is crucial. When someone is fatigued, it is easy to wear their emotions on their sleeve. And when things aren’t going particularly well, it’s very easy to think that things are going worse than they actually are. If you can not only be a voice of reason, but also lift an athlete’s spirits while doing so, you can help them reframe their current situation, thus helping them start to build positive momentum. CTS coaches like to use this saying with athletes in a crewing context: “It doesn’t always get worse.” It’s my favorite way to help an athlete reframe their current situation and share a positive sentiment. While acknowledging the current scenario may not be ideal, the trail ahead is an unknown, and that unknown has the possibility of being positive in the future.

    In a recent development, effective communication is not only important for physical support, but emotional support as well. At each crewing opportunity, start by asking yourself these  questions before jumping into action:.

    Whether the athlete needs you to give them some tough love or to be their biggest cheerleader, having a calm demeanor, bringing positive energy, and being an effective communicator can turn a DNF into a salvaged race they can be proud of for years to come.

    Recent findings suggest that crewing’s a simple task but requires a lot of preparation both before and during the event. The more you do it, the more comfortable and efficient you’ll get at it. The long days at Foresthill, Javelina Jeadquarters, and Champex-Lac preparing for an athlete’s arrival and executing a top-notch crewing job is one of the most satisfying things I do as a coach. I hope this framework gives you upcoming perspectives on how to best go about crewing, a few more things to add to your gear list, and helps you enjoy the process of crewing more by knowing that you’re prepared and making the right decisions each step of the way.

    • The Stifel Killington Cup returns to Killington, Vt., Thanksgiving weekend, welcoming some of the world’s best women ski racers back to U.S.
    • In a recent development, the two-day Stifel Killington Cup features women’s giant slalom on Saturday (Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, mikaela Shiffrin during Copper Media Days on November 17, 2026 at Copper Mountain in Frisco, Colorado. Photo: Matan Coll // U.S. Ski Team @matancoll (Photo: Matan Coll // U.S. Ski & Snowboard).

    The Stifel Killington Cup returns to Killington, Vt., Thanksgiving weekend, welcoming some of the world’s best women ski racers back to U.S. soil. For the American women, in particular, there’s plenty to be excited about.

    In a recent development, the two-day Stifel Killington Cup features women’s giant slalom on Saturday (Nov. 28), followed by slalom on Sunday (Nov. 29). It’s the first time the World Cup has visited Killington since 2024, when Mikaela Shiffrin crashed on a steep portion of the giant slalom course and suffered a deep puncture wound to the abdomen.

    This time around, Shiffrin returns as a three-time Olympic gold medalist, the winningest Alpine ski racer in history, and one of the favorites in both disciplines. But she’s not the only American worth watching. A strong U.S. squad includes a rising slalom talent and an athlete who arrives in Vermont fresh off the biggest victory of her career so far.

    In a recent development, there’s no question who will draw the biggest crowd. Mikaela Shiffrin has won 110 World Cup races and three Olympic gold medals, and she has stood atop the Killington podium six times, including four consecutive slalom victories from 2016 to 2019.

    It has been revealed that she arrives in Vermont following another impressive season, highlighted by a gold medal in slalom at the 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics. She’s also coming off an impressive stretch of technical racing: Shiffrin won her last five slalom starts, including the Olympics, and has finished on the podium in 14 consecutive slaloms dating back to February 2025.

    Sunday’s race carries particular significance. Shiffrin has indicated that she’ll be selective about her slalom appearances this season, and Killington is expected to be her first slalom start of the winter. It’s a fitting place for her return to the discipline following her 2024 crash on the final pitch before the finish line on her second run. She lost control on the steep section of the Superstar course, slid into a gate, and punctured her oblique muscles. Shiffrin underwent surgery to clean and close the wound, followed by months of rehabilitation before returning to competition in February 2025.

    In addition to the physical toll of the injury, the episode shook the ski racer’s confidence, and it took time for her to get back to her competitive rhythm. But in typical Shiffrin fashion, she went on to reclaim her place atop the sport, eventually adding another Olympic slalom gold medal to her collection in 2026.

    If anyone can challenge Shiffrin for the spotlight, it’s Moltzan. The 32-year-old Minnesota native is coming off the best start to a World Cup season of her career, having captured her first-ever World Cup victory in the giant slalom in Sölden, Austria, on Oct. 24.

    It has been revealed that moltzan’s breakthrough win was a long time coming. A consistent contender on the World Cup circuit, she has steadily established herself as one of America’s strongest technical racers. She also earned an Olympic bronze medal in the team combined at the 2026 Games, further cementing her place among the country’s top Alpine racers.

    With confidence from her first World Cup victory and a strong history of giant slalom results, Moltzan is a legitimate podium threat on Saturday. She’ll also be one to watch in Sunday’s slalom.

    Industry observers note that keep an eye on 25-year-old AJ Hurt, who’s emerging as another key piece of the American technical team. Hurt has been particularly impressive in slalom this season, finishing fourth at Gurgl, Austria, and 15th at Levi, Finland, earlier this month. She was the top American woman in both races.

    That fourth-place finish at Gurgl was especially encouraging, putting Hurt within striking distance of her first-ever World Cup podium. She’s shown the ability to ski aggressively against the world’s best, and another strong performance in Killington could be a significant step forward.

    It has been revealed that other American technical racers, including Nina O’Brien and Katie Hensien, are also worth following as the start lists take shape. O’Brien has established herself as a strong giant slalom competitor, while Hensien brings additional technicality to the U.S. slalom squad.

    Both days of racing will be broadcast live on NBC and Peacock, with first runs available on Peacock and NBCSN. Saturday’s women’s giant slalom begins at 9:30 a.m. ET, with the second run at 12:30 p.m. ET.

    According to recent reports, sunday’s slalom starts at 10:30 a.m. ET, followed by the final run at 1 p.m. ET. For viewers who can’t tune in live, Peacock will also offer streaming access to the races.

    #147915. On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (873 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun.
    • According to recent reports, there is a cinema up north.
    • In a recent development, this is a film review of sorts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun).

    According to recent reports, there is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

    In a recent development, this is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

    There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

    If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

    “Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

    Recent findings suggest that but can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

    I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

    According to recent reports, however, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

    Industry observers note that I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a big-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

    Industry observers note that my reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

    I watched The Alpinist on the massive screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

    According to recent reports, but anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”.

    According to recent reports, from my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

    Industry observers note that nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

    Kiprun Kipsummit Race Review: We Tested the Trail Super Shoe That Won the 2026 Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (912 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
    • Industry observers note that when Blandine L’Hirondel crossed the finish line first at the 2026 Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc, the buzz was not only about her record-breaking 21:54:49 but also about what shoes she was wearing.
    • The debut racer, also the least expensive shoe on the podium at $250, clearly held its own in a field of tried-and-proven competitors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

    Industry observers note that when Blandine L’Hirondel crossed the finish line first at the 2026 Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc, the buzz was not only about her record-breaking 21:54:49 but also about what shoes she was wearing. L’Hirondel is a name the trail running world knows well. Her sponsor, Kiprun, isn’t, especially in the United States. Kiprun is the running brand of Decathlon, the French sporting goods giant, and the shoe on L’Hirondel’s feet was its first carbon-plated trail racer, the Kipsummit Race.

    The debut racer, also the least expensive shoe on the podium at $250, clearly held its own in a field of tried-and-proven competitors. Runner-up Rachel Entrekin’s Norda 055, for example, retails for $325. Other models on the podium ranged from $260 to $280.

    For the last three months, I’ve been testing the Kiprun Kipsummit Race to find out firsthand what this new $250 trail super shoe can do.

    Weight: 9 oz (men’s 8); 7.8 oz (women’s 5) Stack Height: 37.5–31.5 mm Heel-to-Toe Drop: 6 mm Lug Depth: 4 mm.

    + One of the lightest carbon trail racers + Firm, responsive midsole doesn’t feel mushy + Confidence-inspiring stability and grip, especially on descents – Stiff sole and upper need a break-in period – Not ideal for very technical, rocky terrain.

    I was first introduced to Kiprun at The Running Event in December 2025, a trade show for run specialty retailers and brands. I was immediately drawn to the Kipsummit Race, the brand’s marquee carbon-plated trail shoe, and couldn’t wait to test it. Nearly nine months later, Blandine L’Hirondel wore it to her record-setting win at UTMB. Coincidentally (or not?), my sample pair arrived in the mail just after the win.

    From the moment I picked it up, the Kipsummit Race felt remarkably light. At 9 ounces for a men’s 8 and 7.8 ounces for a women’s 5, it’s one of the lightest carbon-plated trail shoes you can buy. Fittingly, the only other shoe as lightweight is the Asics Metafuji Trail 2, which Ben Dhiman wore to win the men’s race at UTMB.

    The Kipsummit Race has one of the toughest uppers I’ve tested. The patented upper material (a blend of polyester, thermoplastic polyurethane, and polyamide) is lightweight and extremely durable, with a stiff, structured feel that really holds the foot in place once the laces are cinched. It’s not the coziest feel out of the box, but over time, it broke in and felt more comfortable.

    Underfoot, the ATPU midsole uses an embedded, full-length, forked carbon fiber plate to create a rigid, rockered sole. Most of the ATPU midsoles I’ve tested have been in road shoes, and tend to be very soft. The Kipsummit Race was not. The shoe felt firmer than I expected during my first test run on a crushed gravel path outside Philadelphia. That wasn’t necessarily a bad thing: It was firm, but it had a responsive pop, and I didn’t notice any sinking into the midsole or instability on stance and push-off.

    On another test run in Santa Barbara, California, I climbed about 1,200 feet up a dirt fire road. It was rutted and rocky from water runoff, but the shoe remained stable on the uneven terrain. The firmer midsole, paired with a wide base, felt grounded, and the forked plate, with a cut-out under the heel, kept my foot centered. When I needed to navigate through technical terrain, however, the thick, wide profile and lack of ground feel wasn’t ideal.

    It has been revealed that the Kipsummit Race really shone on the descent. The Vibram Megagrip Litebase outsole with 4 millimeter lugs gripped loose rock and kitty litter with confidence, while still being mild enough to run on roads for long stretches. I’m not naturally a strong downhill runner, but I felt safe going beyond my comfort zone, which I attribute to the combination of great grip, a firmly stable midsole, a wide base, and a secure upper.

    Industry observers note that the one thing I didn’t get to test is how comfortable the shoe, with its firmer midsole and stiff upper, feels over ultra distances. The shoe started to break in with more use, so you may need to log more miles in it to feel its true comfort. Kiprun boasts that it holds up for more than 1,000 kilometers (about 620 miles), and given that L’Hirondel trusted one pair for the entire UTMB, that tracks.

    Like carbon fiber road racing shoes, carbon fiber trail shoes have a reputation for being made only for fast, strong, competitive runners. That reputation may be earned on the road, but I don’t think it’s true for trail shoes. There isn’t nearly as much research showing that carbon fiber trail shoes provide any performance benefit to trail runners, elite or beginner—the plates function as much for protection and stability as they do for propulsion.

    That said, plated trail shoes offer a different running experience than non-plated shoes. If that feels good to you, then wear them. This is my long way of saying that the Kiprun Kipsummit Race is suitable for any runner who likes a stiffer shoe, both in flex and cushioning, that holds up to high mileage. It’s best suited for smooth to moderately technical terrain, and for anything from short trail races to 100-milers.

    #147912. Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1093 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

    Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1093 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage.
    • When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.
    • In a recent development, “All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he indicates.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage. (Photo: Courtesy Ben Zartman).

    When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.

    In a recent development, “All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he indicates. “Most of the guys at the crag were sewing their own shoes or making their own cams.” Backpacks, harnesses, quickdraws—if they could sew it themselves, they did. At the time, Zartman was in high school. He didn’t have a job, but he did have a knack for making stuff. It never occurred to him that doing so might be sketchy until he arrived in Yosemite for the first time in 1995 and partners refused to climb on his rack. They were astonished he’d made his own gear. He was astonished that they’d bought theirs.

    Sources indicate that later that year, when a government shutdown forced Zartman out of Joshua Tree, he hitchhiked to San Diego and bummed a ride to Baja with some sailors. Over the next few years, he split his time between major walls and boats, getting better at both kinds of rigging all the while. Then he got married, had three daughters, and spent five years sailing around the world on a boat he’d built himself. Eventually, he got work in a rigging shop in Rhode Island. He spliced custom slings for workaday sailors, then for open-ocean racing boats.

    “At one point, I was sitting in the shop, splicing these high-end Dyneema loops, and I thought, man, if I had these in Yosemite, I would have been the coolest kid at the lodge cafeteria,” he states. And he likely would have: the spliced, covered loops used in sailing are seamless: no bar tacks or stitching. Instead, one end of the loop is woven into the other like a snake eating its tail. When you pull, the ends suction against each other (Zartman compares it to a finger-trap toy), making the loop stronger under load than bartacked Dyneema.

    “The idea fomented for a while in my mind, and in 2021 I started reaching out to every climbing gear manufacturer I could think of,” Zartman indicates. Letters and samples went out to Black Diamond, Metolius, Sterling, and others, asking them if they’d be interested in partnering on a product. Hardly anyone responded.

    So Zartman did what he’d always done: he took the DIY approach. In 2023, he debuted his company, Zartman Rigging. He joined the UIAA, mailed in slings for lab testing, and registered for UIAA labels. Once his gear was certified, the renowned gear shop IME, in North Conway, Newly introduced Hampshire, started selling it. Rock and Snow in New Paltz, New York, and IME in Salt Lake City, Utah, were next. As his following grew, so did his offerings: a featherlight personal anchor system, seamless rappel back-ups, a rope-carabiner alternative called the Dreamlink, and a tiny rappel plate designed for 6-mm cord. The ideas come from Zartman’s experience climbing Yosemite walls; the materials come from his time on boats.

    “The research and development budget in the [sailboat] racing scene is so significant,” he states. “It’s a great place to take technology from. I’m at that edge—I make ropes for the fanciest racing boats in the world, so I’m able to bring that into the climbing world pretty rapidly.”.

    The results are wild. The Dreamlink has a breaking strength of 43 kN (or, rather, he tested it up to 42 kN in a UIAA lab, and that’s when it broke their machine). The seamless runners are tagged 24 kN but break at 27kN. A fancy UV coating makes them essentially sun-proof. They don’t expire like other soft goods; you only have to retire them if the core becomes exposed. I have a double-length seamless runner that I use for building anchors and extending rappels. No bartack means easy setup, it racks well, and it’s pretty light. (Most traditionally manufactured Dyneema slings are tagged at 22kN. Mammut’s 120-centimeter Contact Sling weighs 28 grams, while Zartman’s version is 32 grams, the same as Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord.).

    Industry observers note that zartman has a strong social media fan club, but he has plenty of critics too. Mountain Project commenters, he remarked, can be particularly vicious. Many scoff at the idea of a soft shackle or a seamless runner as gimmicky or unsafe. He’s not too bothered.

    “Ray Jardine got scolded by all the Valley locals when he demonstrated up with Friends,” he indicates, citing the first-ever cams. When other companies started making camming devices in the ‘80s, Jardine’s critics were forced to bite their tongues. Zartman is seeing a similar arc with his own gear. Several other climbing brands have started marketing soft shackles similar to Zartman’s Dreamlink. And in 2025, Black Diamond released its Infinity Cord, a Dyneema sling that uses the same bartack-free construction as Zartman’s and the same covered-loop splicing technique that sailors have used for decades. Black Diamond called it a “breakthrough in the evolution of cordelette engineering.”.

    Industry observers note that zartman says he’s unaffected by the fresh competition. “If there are people copying the concept, that’s good because that means the concept is good,” he says. In the meantime, he’s keeping his head down, focused on fulfilling orders and prototyping his next batch of inventions.

    Zartman Rigging is gaining recognition, albeit slowly. Zartman does no paid advertising; about 80 percent of his business comes from Instagram. His top-shelf pricing likely tempers growth as well. For context, a 120-centimeter Zartman Rigging sling is $63, versus $40 for Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord or $14 for a basic Dyneema Trango runner of the same length.

    In a recent development, “Because I make everything out of the nicest materials and by hand, it’s the most expensive gear on the market. It’s a luxury brand,” he claims. “Which is ironic given that I started in Mexico with my own homemade climbing shoes.”.

    Still, he produces enough to keep busy. Recently, he was able to hire one of his daughters part-time to help him splice, tag, and quality-test each product. He’s now a member of the UIAA safety commission, helping the organization design fresh testing protocols around skinny ropes and other novel forms of cord. He’s shipping to Alaska and Hawaii. People have started recognizing him in gear shops and at crags. Things are taking off—despite what Mountain Projectors may say.
